title: French at Home
pronunciation_guide: English-friendly respelling for standard French, written once per phrase in tools/fr-pronunciation.json. No capitals: French gives every syllable about the same weight. Linked words are joined with hyphens.

phrases.note: Lève-toi comes from se lever (to get up, literally 'to lift yourself'). In a command, toi goes after the verb with a hyphen.
C'est l'heure de + a verb = It's time to... Swap the verb: c'est l'heure de manger (time to eat).
Sors is the tu command of sortir (to go out). Du = de + le, so du lit means 'out of the bed'.

phrases.fr: Sors du lit, tout de suite.
phrases.ph: sor dew lee, too duh sweet
phrases.note: Tout de suite = straight away. It's the go-to phrase for 'right now!' when a parent has run out of patience.
Allez comes from aller (to go) but here just means 'come on'. It's a fixed expression, so you say allez even to one person.
En retard = late (for something). Tu vas + a verb = you're going to... — the easy way to talk about the future.
Déjà = already, and it sits right after the verb: tu es déjà... Don't mix up en retard (late for something) with tard (late in the day).
Réveillée has an extra -e because it's said to a girl; to a boy it's réveillé. Both sound exactly the same.
In the past tense (tu as dormi = you slept), short words like bien squeeze in between as and dormi.

phrases.en: What time did you go to sleep?
phrases.fr: Tu t'es endormie à quelle heure ?
phrases.note: S'endormir = to fall asleep. It uses être in the past, so a girl is endormie and a boy endormi. À quelle heure ? = at what time?
French 'takes' a shower: prendre une douche. Pris is the past form of prendre, so tu as pris = you have taken.
Va is the tu command of aller, with no s. Va + a verb = go and do something: va manger, va dormir.
S'habiller = to get dressed, literally 'to dress yourself'. Habiller on its own means to dress someone else, like a baby.
Habillée ends in -ée because it's asked to a girl; ask a boy Tu es habillé ? The two sound identical.
Literally 'you brushed yourself the teeth'. French says les dents, not tes dents, because t' already shows they're yours.
Se coiffer = to do your hair (un coiffeur is a hairdresser). Coiffée has -ée for a girl; a boy is coiffé.
Tout = everything, and its final t is silent. Tu as tout ? is the quick check before anyone leaves the house.
Où with an accent means 'where'; ou without one means 'or'. Chaussures is plural, so it's sont and tes.
Manteau is masculine (le manteau), so 'your' is ton. Où est... ? = Where is...? — works for anything you've lost.
N'oublie pas = don't forget. In tu commands, -er verbs drop their s: tu oublies becomes oublie.
Le déjeuner = lunch in France. Careful: le petit-déjeuner (the 'little lunch') is breakfast.
Un portable is a mobile phone — the word just means 'portable'. Lots of French teens shorten it to mon tél.
Une clé (a key) is feminine. You may also see it spelt clef — same word, same sound.

phrases.en: What time do you need to leave?
phrases.fr: Tu dois partir à quelle heure ?
phrases.note: Tu dois + a verb = you have to... It comes from devoir (must) — the same word as les devoirs, homework.

phrases.en: What time do you need to be there?
phrases.fr: Tu dois y être à quelle heure ?
phrases.note: Y means 'there' and goes before the verb: y être = to be there. It's tiny but everywhere: j'y vais = I'm going (there).
Prête is for a girl — a boy says prêt, and then the t is silent.
Presque = nearly, almost. It goes just before the word it changes: presque prête, presque fini.
Allez ! is also the football chant: Allez les Bleus ! (Come on France!). The louder and longer, the less patience is left.
Se dépêcher = to hurry. Dépêche-toi is for one person; to several people it's dépêchez-vous.
On means 'we' in everyday French and takes the same verb form as il/elle: on doit, on va. Y aller = to go (there).
Attendre = to wait for — the 'for' is built in, so no extra word. T' (you) goes before the verb.
Tout le monde = everyone (literally 'all the world'). It counts as one, so the verb is attend, not attendent.
Dans + time = in that much time from now. En cinq minutes would mean 'it takes five minutes'.
Like English, French uses the present (on part = we leave) for something about to happen. Maintenant = now.
Monter = to go up, but also to get into a car, bus or train. The opposite is descendre (to get out).
Bonjour covers 'good morning' and 'hello' all day long. 'Bon matin' isn't used in France.
Un réveil is an alarm clock, from se réveiller (to wake up). Sonner = to ring — also used for a doorbell or phone.
Entendre = to hear; entendu is its past form. Don't confuse it with attendre (to wait) — only one letter apart.
Se rendormir = to fall back asleep; re- means 'again', as in English. In a 'don't' command, te stays before the verb.

phrases.fr: La salle de bains est libre.
phrases.ph: la sal duh ban ay leebr
phrases.note: La salle de bains is the room with the bath or shower. In French homes the toilet is often a separate room: les toilettes.
Meals use prendre (to take): prendre son petit-déjeuner = to have breakfast.

phrases.en: Have some breakfast before you go.
phrases.fr: Mange quelque chose avant de partir.
phrases.ph: mahnzh kel-kuh shohz a-vahn duh par-teer
phrases.note: Avant de + a verb = before doing something: avant de partir (before leaving). The verb stays in its basic 'to' form.
Mettre = to put, and also to put on clothes. Mets keeps its s in the command because mettre isn't an -er verb.
Mets ton... works for any clothes: mets ton pull, mets ton écharpe. To take it off: enlève ton manteau.
Propre = clean, not 'proper'. Most French schools have no uniform, so this is a very British question!
Encore = more, again or still. Encore cinq minutes is the classic lie-in plea; encore une fois = one more time.
Va-t'en comes from s'en aller (to go away). Blunt — fine with family, but rude to anyone else.
Dehors = outside. Shouted on its own it means 'Out!' — very blunt, the kind of thing you'd say to Monty the dog.
Une chambre is a bedroom, not any room — a room in general is une pièce. Chambre is feminine, so ma.
Fatiguée has -ée because the speaker is a girl; a boy says fatigué. You can't hear the difference.
Crevée is slang for 'shattered' (literally 'burst', like a tyre). Fine at home; a boy says crevé.
Here levée means 'out of bed', from se lever; a boy says levé. Add déjà for extra attitude: Je suis déjà levée !
C'est bon here means 'All right, all right!' — an annoyed way of saying stop nagging. Je me lève = I'm getting up.
Arrête de + a verb = stop doing something. Reuse it: arrête de parler, arrête de m'embêter (stop annoying me).

phrases.fr: Je ne trouve pas mes chaussures.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh troov pa may shoh-sewr
phrases.note: Trouver = to find. French doesn't need 'can' here: je ne trouve pas simply means 'I can't find'.

phrases.fr: Où est ma brosse à cheveux ?
phrases.ph: oo ay ma bros a shuh-vuh
phrases.note: Une brosse à cheveux = a brush for hair. À links an object to its use: une brosse à dents is a toothbrush.
Tranquille = calm, quiet, so it's literally 'leave me calm'. Normal at home; Fiche-moi la paix ! is ruder.
Tôt = early; its opposite is tard (late). Il est is used for time: il est tôt, il est sept heures.
French says 'I don't have hunger', using avoir (to have). Same with thirst: j'ai soif = I'm thirsty.
J'arrive literally means 'I'm arriving', but it's what the French shout for 'I'm coming!' — even while still in bed.
Éteindre = to switch off (and to put out a fire). The opposite is allumer: allume la lumière = turn the light on.
Un rideau = a curtain. Words ending in -eau add x, not s, in the plural: des rideaux, des gâteaux.

phrases.fr: Je n'ai pas dormi du tout.
phrases.ph: zhuh nay pa dor-mee dew too
phrases.note: Pas du tout = not at all. Put du tout at the end to make any 'not' stronger: je n'aime pas du tout ça.

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.fr: Je ne veux pas aller au collège.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh vuh pa a-lay oh ko-lezh
phrases.note: False friend: le collège is secondary school for 11 to 15-year-olds, not college. Older teens go to le lycée.

phrases.fr: Je ne me sens pas bien.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh muh sahn pa byan
phrases.note: Se sentir = to feel. Ne ... pas wraps around me sens, so this is 'I don't feel well'.

phrases.fr: Il y a quelqu'un dans la salle de bains !
phrases.ph: eel-ya kel-kuhn dahn la sal duh ban
phrases.note: Il y a = there is or there are. Quelqu'un = someone — the apostrophe replaces the e of quelque.

phrases.en: He's been in there for ages!
phrases.fr: Ça fait des heures qu'il est dedans !
phrases.note: Ça fait + time + que = it's been... French uses the present (il est) where English says 'has been'.

phrases.en: Who used all the hot water?
phrases.fr: Qui a pris toute l'eau chaude ?
phrases.ph: kee a pree toot loh shohd
phrases.note: L'eau (water) is feminine, so both words describing it agree: toute and chaude. Pris here means 'used up'.

phrases.en: Can you take me in the car?
phrases.note: Tu peux ... ? = Can you ...? Emmener = to take someone somewhere; en voiture = by car.
Le lundi with le means 'on Mondays' in general. Days of the week don't take a capital letter in French.

phrases.fr: Dépêche-toi dans la salle de bains !
phrases.ph: day-pesh twa dahn la sal duh ban
phrases.note: Dans = in (inside a place). Dépêche-toi drops the s of tu te dépêches, like every -er verb command.

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.fr: Tu en as pour combien de temps ?
phrases.ph: tew ahn-na poor kohn-byan duh tahn
phrases.note: En avoir pour + time = to need that long: j'en ai pour deux minutes (I'll be two minutes). Combien de temps = how long.

phrases.fr: Les autres aussi ont besoin de la salle de bains.
phrases.ph: lay-zohtr oh-see ohn buh-zwan duh la sal duh ban
phrases.note: Avoir besoin de = to need (literally 'to have need of'). Les autres = the others, everyone else.

phrases.fr: Tu ne vas pas sortir comme ça.
phrases.ph: tew nuh va pa sor-teer kom sa
phrases.note: Literally 'You're not going out like that.' Comme ça = like that — a firm parent's no.
Jolie = pretty, for a girl. To a boy, say Tu es très beau; Tu es très belle is a bigger compliment for a girl.
Tagging ça onto the end adds a raised-eyebrow feel: 'Is it clean, that?' Very common in spoken French.
Un sèche-cheveux is literally a 'dry-hair': sécher (to dry) + cheveux (hair). Same pattern as un lave-vaisselle, a dishwasher.
Baisser = to lower, turn down; to turn it up is monter. Baisse le son (turn the sound down) is also common.

phrases.en: You've been in there for ages.
phrases.fr: Ça fait une heure que tu es là-dedans.
phrases.ph: sa feh-tewn-ur kuh tew ay la-duh-dahn
phrases.note: Là-dedans = in there. French parents exaggerate too: une heure (an hour) here really just means 'ages'.
Ouvrir ends in -ir but behaves like an -er verb: tu ouvres, and the command ouvre has no s.

phrases.en: Put a jumper on, it's cold.
phrases.fr: Mets un pull, il fait froid.
phrases.note: Il fait froid = it's cold. French uses faire (to do/make) for weather: il fait chaud, il fait beau. Un pull is a jumper.
Jupe is feminine, so cette (that) and courte (short) both take their feminine form. Trop = too.
Trop de = too much or too many, and it's always de, never du: trop de bruit, trop de devoirs.

phrases.en: Don't leave your towel on the floor.
phrases.fr: Ne laisse pas ta serviette par terre.
phrases.ph: nuh les pa ta sehr-vyet par tehr
phrases.note: Par terre = on the floor. Careful: une serviette is a towel, but at the table it's a napkin.
Un haut = a top (haut means high). Its h stops sounds linking, so the n of mon doesn't run into haut.

phrases.en: Your clothes are on the chair.
phrases.fr: Tes vêtements sont sur la chaise.
phrases.ph: tay vet-mahn sohn sewr la shez
phrases.note: Les vêtements = clothes. The ê marks an s that used to be there — think of English 'vestments'.

phrases.en: It's still in the washing machine.
phrases.fr: C'est encore dans la machine à laver.
phrases.ph: say-tahn-kor dahn la ma-sheen a la-vay
phrases.note: La machine à laver = 'the machine for washing'. Lots of families just say la machine: c'est dans la machine.
Autre chose = something else, with no un or une in front: mets autre chose, fais autre chose.
Ne ... plus = not any more, no longer. It wraps round the verb just like ne ... pas.

phrases.fr: Ça va comme ça, tu es très bien !
phrases.ph: sa va kom sa, tew ay treh byan
phrases.note: Tu es très bien = you look great — bien can describe how someone looks. Ça va comme ça = it's fine as it is.
Me shrinks to m' before a vowel: je m'habille. Shout it through the door to stop anyone barging in.
Je prends = I take or I'm taking. To stress 'right now', say je suis en train de prendre ma douche.
French says 'under the shower': sous la douche. Dans la douche sounds odd to a French ear.
Je me coiffe comes from se coiffer. The me shows you're doing it to yourself, so no word for 'hair' is needed.
Se maquiller = to put on makeup; le maquillage is the makeup itself. Se démaquiller = to take it off.
Same pattern for other body parts: je me lave les mains (I'm washing my hands), je me brosse les cheveux.
Prête (girl) and prêt (boy) sound different: in prête you hear the t, in prêt you don't.

phrases.en: I'll be ready in five minutes.
phrases.fr: Je serai prête dans cinq minutes.
phrases.ph: zhuh suh-reh pret dahn sank mee-newt
phrases.note: Serai is the future of être: je serai = I will be. A boy says je serai prêt.
Minute is feminine, so it's une minute. You'll also hear Deux secondes ! (two seconds) for the same idea.
Laisse-moi = let me, give me. In a command, me becomes moi and goes after the verb with a hyphen.
Attends is the tu command of attendre. Verbs ending in -re keep their s in commands: attends, descends, réponds.
J'arrive (from arriver) is the standard reply when someone calls you. Add tout de suite for 'right now!'.

phrases.en: I'll be there in a minute.
phrases.fr: Je suis là dans une minute.
phrases.note: Là can mean here or there. French often uses the present (je suis) for the near future, where English says 'I'll be'.
Descendre = to go down; monter = to go up. French doesn't need a word for 'stairs' here.
Les fringues is casual slang for clothes: Où sont mes fringues ? Vêtements is the everyday word.
Un sweat (from English sweatshirt) is what French teens call a hoodie; the full name is un sweat à capuche.
A pair of jeans is un jean — singular in French. Tu as vu ... ? = Have you seen ...?
Chaussures = shoes in general; trainers are des baskets. Où sont mes baskets ? is what many teens would actually say.
Ça = this or that. No question word needed — just raise your voice at the end to make it a question.
Sec = dry; for a feminine noun it becomes sèche (ma chemise est sèche). The opposite is mouillé, wet.
Laver = to wash something; se laver = to wash yourself. Tu peux + a verb = Can you...?
En stands for 'of it' after avoir besoin de: j'en ai besoin = I need it. Pour demain = for tomorrow.
Sors de... = get out of... Swap the place: sors de la salle de bains, sors de la cuisine.
Add s'il te plaît to sound much nicer. Use s'il te plaît with tu and s'il vous plaît with vous.
Entrer = to come or go in. Ne shortens to n' before a vowel, and the pair wraps around the verb: n'entre pas.
Se changer = to get changed (your clothes). Without se, changer just means to change something.

phrases.fr: Il y a quelqu'un dans la salle de bains.
phrases.ph: eel-ya kel-kuhn dahn la sal duh ban
phrases.note: Il y a quelqu'un ? on its own is what you call out to check a room: 'Is anyone in there?'

phrases.en: Are you going to be long in the bathroom?
phrases.fr: Tu en as encore pour longtemps dans la salle de bains ?
phrases.ph: tew ahn-na-zahn-kor poor lohn-tahn dahn la sal duh ban
phrases.note: Longtemps = a long time. Encore adds 'still', so it's 'are you still going to be long?'

phrases.fr: Il n'y a pas d'eau chaude.
phrases.note: After pas, de l' becomes just d': il y a de l'eau, but il n'y a pas d'eau.
Les cheveux = the hair on your head, and it's always plural in French: mes cheveux sont mouillés (my hair is wet).

phrases.fr: Il n'y a plus de shampoing.
phrases.note: Il n'y a plus de... = there's no more... — the handy way to say 'we've run out of...'.

phrases.fr: Il n'y a pas de papier toilette.
phrases.ph: eel nya pa duh pa-pyay twa-let
phrases.note: Papier toilette is what families say; papier hygiénique is more formal. The room itself is plural: les toilettes.

phrases.en: Does this look OK on me?
phrases.note: Aller à quelqu'un = to suit someone. Ça me va bien ? = Does it suit me? The answer: ça te va bien.

phrases.fr: Je n'ai rien à me mettre.
phrases.note: Ne ... rien = nothing. Rien à + a verb = nothing to...: rien à faire (nothing to do), rien à manger.
Prêt agrees with le petit-déjeuner, which is masculine. With a feminine noun it's prête: la soupe est prête.
Many French parents just shout À table ! (to the table!) to call everyone for any meal.
Le dîner is the evening meal in France. Prêt (ready) matches le dîner; a feminine word would take prête: la soupe est prête.
French families just say C'est prêt ! (It's ready!). The other classic call is À table ! – literally 'to the table!'
No word for 'and' here: French puts the second verb straight after venir. Viens voir = come and see, viens m'aider = come and help me.
Se servir means 'to help yourself' (to food), literally 'to serve yourself'. Sers-toi ! on its own = Help yourself!

phrases.en: What do you want for breakfast?
phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu veux pour le petit-déjeuner ?
phrases.ph: kes-kuh tew vuh poor luh puh-tee-day-zhuh-nay
phrases.note: Petit-déjeuner is literally 'little lunch'. Qu'est-ce que tu veux ... ? = What do you want ...? – a pattern you can reuse all day.

phrases.en: What do you want for lunch?
phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu veux pour le déjeuner ?
phrases.ph: kes-kuh tew vuh poor luh day-zhuh-nay
phrases.note: Le déjeuner is lunch in France (it's the midday meal). As a verb, déjeuner means 'to have lunch': on déjeune à midi.
French says 'you have hunger': avoir faim. Never say 'tu es faim'. Same with thirst: tu as soif ?

phrases.en: Do you want something to eat?
phrases.fr: Tu veux quelque chose à manger ?
phrases.ph: tew vuh kel-kuh shohz a mahn-zhay
phrases.note: Quelque chose à + verb = something to ... : quelque chose à boire, quelque chose à lire. Tu veux ... ? is the everyday way to offer.
Literally 'you want to drink something?' – that's how French offers a drink. Une boisson is 'a drink' as a noun, but it sounds stiffer here.

phrases.en: What do you want to drink?
phrases.note: Boire = to drink. In quick speech families often flip it round: Tu veux boire quoi ? Both mean the same.
De l' means 'some' before a vowel: de l'eau. French needs this little word where English can drop 'some' – never just 'tu veux eau'.
Reprendre = to take again, so to have seconds. En means 'some of it' and sits before the verb: tu en reprends ?
Suffire = to be enough, so 'is that enough for you?'. Careful: Ça suffit ! on its own is what an annoyed parent shouts – 'That's enough!'
Terminer = to finish, just like finir. The past is made with avoir: tu as terminé, literally 'you have finished'.
Mange is the command form of manger. With tu, -er verbs lose the final s in a command: tu manges → Mange !
Goûter = to taste or try food. Au moins = at least. Le goûter is also the after-school snack French children have at about 4 pm.
Watch the spelling: the command is goûte, but before en it gets its s back to help the sound – goûtes-en (try some of it).

phrases.fr: Tu n'y as même pas goûté.
phrases.ph: tew nee a mem pa goo-tay
phrases.note: Même pas = not even. French says goûter à quelque chose, so 'it' becomes y (to it): tu n'y as pas goûté.
To say 'don't' in a command, wrap the verb in ne ... pas: ne mange pas, ne touche pas, ne cours pas.
Presque = nearly, almost. It slots in just before the adjective, like in English: presque fini, presque prêt.

phrases.en: It'll be ready in ten minutes.
phrases.fr: Ce sera prêt dans dix minutes.
phrases.ph: suh suh-ra preh dahn dee mee-newt
phrases.note: Sera is the future of être (will be). Dans + time = in ... time from now: dans dix minutes, dans une heure.

phrases.en: Put your plate in the dishwasher.
phrases.fr: Mets ton assiette dans le lave-vaisselle.
phrases.note: Une assiette is a plate – it's feminine but takes ton, not ta, because it starts with a vowel. Lave-vaisselle = 'wash-dishes'.
La poubelle is the bin. French says à la poubelle (to the bin), not dans. Mets comes from mettre, to put.

phrases.en: Put it back in the fridge.
phrases.note: Re- on a verb often means 'again' or 'back': mettre = put, remettre = put back. Le frigo is the everyday word for le réfrigérateur.
Tu peux ... ? = Can you ...? – the easiest way to ask for help. Mettre la table (put the table) means to lay it.
Débarrasser = to clear away. You'll also hear se débarrasser de, to get rid of something.
Vider = to empty; the adjective vide means empty. The opposite, remplir, means to fill.
French doesn't really 'load' a dishwasher – it fills it: remplir. You'll also hear mettre la vaisselle dans le lave-vaisselle.
Laisser = to leave something somewhere. Don't mix it up with partir or quitter, which mean to leave a place.
Le dernier = the last one, for a masculine thing like un biscuit. For a feminine one, like une part de gâteau, it's la dernière.
Là = there, with a grave accent. Without the accent, la means 'the'. Ici = here, là = there.

phrases.en: Wash your hands before you eat.
phrases.fr: Lave-toi les mains avant de manger.
phrases.ph: lav twa lay man a-vahn duh mahn-zhay
phrases.note: Se laver = to wash yourself. French says 'wash yourself the hands', so it's les mains, not tes mains.
Assieds-toi comes from s'asseoir (to sit down). S'il te plaît is for one person you say tu to; to several, use s'il vous plaît.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.fr: Tu peux me passer le sel ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh pa-say luh sel
phrases.note: Me = to me, and it goes before the verb it belongs to: me passer. Swap in le pain, le poivre or l'eau for other things.
Attention ! is how French says 'careful!' or 'watch out!'. Chaud = hot; if food burns your mouth, say ça brûle.
Said by everyone as the meal starts. Link the sounds: the n of bon runs into appétit, so it sounds like 'bo-nappétit'.

phrases.en: Don't eat with your mouth open.
phrases.fr: Ne mange pas la bouche ouverte.
phrases.ph: nuh mahnzh pa la boosh oo-vehrt
phrases.note: French doesn't need 'with your': just la bouche ouverte. Ouverte (open) ends in -e to match la bouche.
Pas de ... = no ... – great for house rules: pas de bonbons, pas d'écrans. À table means 'at the table' at mealtimes.
Il reste = there is ... left, from rester (to remain). False friend: rester means to stay, not to rest.

phrases.fr: Tu m'aides à faire la cuisine ?
phrases.ph: tew med a fehr la kwee-zeen
phrases.note: Aider quelqu'un à + verb = to help someone do something. La cuisine means both the kitchen and cooking.
Plu is the past of plaire (to please), so it's literally 'did it please you?'. It's the natural way to ask if someone enjoyed something.
On (literally 'one') is how French families say 'we' in speech. Ce soir = tonight, this evening.
In chatty French, the question word can go at the end: on mange quand ?, tu rentres quand ? It's casual but completely normal.
Just raise your voice at the end and a statement becomes a question – no need to change the word order.
Quoi = what, placed at the end in relaxed speech. It's the quickest way to ask – fine at home, a bit casual for school.
Literally 'I have hunger' – French uses avoir, not être. Say 'je suis faim' and you'll sound odd.
Literally 'I'm dying of hunger'. Meurs comes from mourir (to die). Dramatic, just like the English.

phrases.fr: Il y a quelque chose à manger ?
phrases.note: Il y a = there is / there are. It never changes for plurals: il y a un biscuit, il y a des biscuits.

phrases.en: Can I have something to eat?
phrases.note: Je peux ... ? = Can I ...? Add any verb after it: je peux sortir ?, je peux regarder la télé ?
Grignoter = to nibble or snack between meals. A snack is un en-cas, but the verb sounds more natural at home.
En = some (of it). It goes before the verb it belongs to, so here it sits after je peux: je peux en reprendre.

phrases.fr: Tu peux me faire quelque chose à manger ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh fehr kel-kuh shohz a mahn-zhay
phrases.note: Faire = to make or to do. Me (for me) goes right before faire. French adds à manger so it's clear you mean food.
On peut ... ? = Can we ...? Much more common at home than nous pouvons. Pizza is feminine: une pizza.
Commander = to order, so 'can we order food?'. Takeaway food is à emporter, which is what you'll see on menus.
Everyone in France calls it le McDo. Au = à + le, so 'to the McDo'.
Ne ... pas wraps round the verb: je n'aime pas. Ne shortens to n' before a vowel. In fast speech the ne often disappears.

phrases.fr: Je ne veux pas de ça.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh vuh pa duh sa
phrases.note: Vouloir de quelque chose is a common way to refuse. A shorter, blunter teen version: J'en veux pas !
Avoir faim (to be hungry) made negative: je n'ai pas faim. Ne becomes n' because ai starts with a vowel.
Déjà = already, and it slots between j'ai and mangé. You'll also hear déjà vu in English – 'already seen'.
Mangerai is the future (I will eat): add -ai to manger. Plus tard = later, literally 'more late'.

phrases.en: Can I eat in my room?
phrases.fr: Je peux manger dans ma chambre ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh mahn-zhay dahn ma shahnbr
phrases.note: La chambre is your bedroom. Watch out: a room in general is une pièce, and une salle is a big room like a classroom.

phrases.fr: Ils sont où, les trucs à grignoter ?
phrases.ph: eel sohn oo, lay trewk a gree-nyo-tay
phrases.note: Un truc = a thing or 'stuff' – super common in spoken French. Trucs à grignoter = things to nibble.
False friend: les chips are crisps! British chips are des frites. Des = some, for plural things.
Du = some, for a masculine thing you can't count: du chocolat, du pain, du fromage. Feminine ones take de la.
La bouffe is slang for food – fine for a cross teenager at home, but say la nourriture or mon repas anywhere polite.
Garder = to keep. Gardais is the 'was ...ing' past tense. Me le = 'it for myself', which makes it sound extra outraged.
Literally 'can I drink something?'. Asking with a verb is more natural than translating 'have a drink' word for word.

phrases.en: Can you get me some water?
phrases.note: Apporter = to bring (a thing). Me becomes m' before the vowel. For bringing a person along, French uses amener.
Bon = good (tasty) for food. Don't use bien here – c'est bien means 'that's good' about a situation or behaviour.
Literally 'I'm no longer hungry' – ne ... plus = no more. Avoid 'je suis pleine': it can mean pregnant (for animals)!

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.note: Just a statement with a questioning voice – 'you pass me the salt?' – which sounds friendly and relaxed at the table.

phrases.fr: Il n'y a plus de lait.
phrases.note: Ne ... plus = no more, not any longer. After a negative, du becomes de: du lait → plus de lait.

phrases.fr: Je peux me faire du pain grillé ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh muh fehr dew pan gree-yay
phrases.note: Toast is du pain grillé (grilled bread). Un toast in French is usually a toast you raise with a glass!
Trop = too (much). Only say this about food or things – for yourself, j'ai trop chaud (I have too much heat).
Cuisiner = to cook. Aider takes à before the next verb: aider à ranger, aider à cuisiner. Te shortens to t' before aider.
C'était = it was, the past of c'est. Délicieux is used for food, so it keeps its masculine form after c'était.
Correctement = properly. Many French adverbs end in -ment, the way English ones end in -ly: lentement, doucement.

phrases.fr: Pas de coudes sur la table.
phrases.ph: pa duh kood sewr la tabl
phrases.note: Un coude is an elbow. Pas de ... = no ..., the short way to set a rule, like 'no elbows on the table'.

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.fr: Ne parle pas la bouche pleine.
phrases.ph: nuh parl pa la boosh plen
phrases.note: Pleine is the feminine of plein (full), matching la bouche. French skips 'with your' and just says la bouche pleine.

phrases.fr: Sers-toi de ton couteau et de ta fourchette.
phrases.ph: sehr twa duh tohn koo-toh ay duh ta foor-shet
phrases.note: Se servir de = to use (literally 'to serve yourself of'). Note ton couteau (masculine) but ta fourchette (feminine).
French says 'finish your plate'. Finis is the command from finir; -ir verbs keep their s in the tu command.
C'est bon ? asks if food tastes good. Careful: gentil means nice about a person, never about food.
Qui = who, and it takes the il form of the verb: qui veut, qui vient. En = some of it; encore = more, again.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the bread?
phrases.fr: Tu peux me passer le pain ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh pa-say luh pan
phrases.note: Le pain = bread; une baguette is the long French loaf. Tu peux me passer ... ? works for anything on the table.
Arrête de + verb = stop doing something. Very handy: arrête de crier, arrête de m'embêter.
En means 'some of it' and never gets left out in French, even though English just says 'want more?'.
Fini is the past form of finir. French says 'you have finished', never 'tu es fini' – that would mean 'you're done for'!

phrases.fr: Attends que tout le monde ait fini.
phrases.ph: a-tahn kuh too luh mohnd eh fee-nee
phrases.note: Tout le monde = everyone (literally 'all the world'). After attendre que, avoir changes to ait – a special form used after certain phrases.
Literally 'take your fork' – prendre is what French parents naturally say. La fourchette is feminine, so ta.
Les légumes = vegetables. Tes is 'your' for plural things, whatever their gender: tes légumes, tes frites.
Ranger = to put away or tidy. Parents often use on (we) to give an order to the whole table without sounding bossy.

phrases.fr: Arrête de jouer avec la nourriture.
phrases.ph: a-ret duh zhoo-ay a-vek la noo-ree-tewr
phrases.note: La nourriture is the proper word for food. French says 'the food' rather than 'your food' here.
Faire sa difficile = to be fussy, literally 'do your difficult one'. To a boy it's ne fais pas ton difficile.

phrases.fr: Il n'y a rien qui cloche.
phrases.note: Clocher is informal for 'to be wrong or off'. Ne ... rien = nothing: il n'y a rien = there's nothing.
Râler = to moan or grumble – the French are famous for it. Un râleur / une râleuse is a moaner.
Literally 'we're not at the restaurant'. Listen for the n' – on n'est sounds just like on est, so it's easy to miss.
Se tenir tranquille = to keep still or behave, literally 'hold yourself calm'. Tranquille looks the same for a boy or a girl.

phrases.fr: Arrête de donner des coups de pied à ton frère.
phrases.ph: a-ret duh do-nay day koo duh pyay a tohn frehr
phrases.note: A kick is un coup de pied, literally 'a hit of foot'. Un coup de poing is a punch (a hit of fist).

phrases.en: Don't feed Monty under the table.
phrases.fr: Ne donne pas à manger à Monty sous la table.
phrases.ph: nuh don pa a mahn-zhay a mohn-tee soo la tabl
phrases.note: Donner à manger à = to feed (literally 'give to eat to'). Sous = under; its opposite is sur (on).
Mâcher = to chew. Fermée (closed) takes an extra -e to agree with la bouche, which is feminine.
S'essuyer = to wipe yourself. Like body-washing verbs, French says 'wipe yourself the mouth': la bouche, not ta bouche.

phrases.en: Say thank you for the food.
phrases.note: Dis is the command from dire (to say). Le repas means the meal – a more natural word than 'food' here.

phrases.fr: Ne tends pas le bras, demande.
phrases.ph: nuh tahn pa luh bra, duh-mahnd
phrases.note: Tendre le bras = to stretch out your arm. False friend: demander means to ask, not to demand.

phrases.fr: Débarrasse ton assiette, s'il te plaît.
phrases.note: Here it means take your plate away, not eat it all. Débarrasser = to clear; assiette is feminine but takes ton before a vowel.
Délicieux ends in -x. For extra praise, French people say C'est trop bon ! – literally 'it's too good'.
Sortir de table is the set phrase for leaving the table. Note: no la – just de table, like à table.
Piquer = to sting, so spicy food 'stings'. Épicé also means spicy, but ça pique is what you'd say mid-mouthful.
In France, pudding means le dessert. Careful: le pudding in French is a specific kind of heavy cake, not afters.

phrases.en: Can I have a bit less?
phrases.fr: Tu peux m'en mettre un peu moins ?
phrases.ph: tew puh mahn metr uhn puh mwan
phrases.note: Un peu moins = a bit less; un peu plus = a bit more. M'en = 'for me, of it', squeezed in before mettre.
Putting ça first adds emphasis: 'this, I don't like'. French often moves the thing to the front to stress it.
Détester = to hate. Blunt, so fine with family but rude if you're a guest. Softer: je n'aime pas trop ça.
Dégoûtant = disgusting. It comes from le goût (taste), so it's literally 'un-tasty'. Rude to say at someone else's house!
Beurk is the French 'yuck!'. For the opposite, say Miam ! Both are just sounds, so they never change.

phrases.en: Why do we keep having this?
phrases.note: Toujours = always. Pourquoi (why) is literally 'for what'. In speech, French keeps normal order after it: pourquoi on mange, not pourquoi mange-t-on.
Encore = again. Pas encore can also mean 'not yet', so the tone of voice does the work here.
Avoir = to have. En (some of it) sits between je peux and avoir – don't drop it, French needs it.
Calé(e) is informal for 'stuffed'. Calée is for a girl – a boy says calé. It also means 'clever' in other contexts.
Literally 'can I go there?' – y aller is the everyday way to say 'go'. On y va ! = Let's go!
Froid = cold. For food it's c'est froid; for yourself it's j'ai froid (I have cold), never je suis froid.
The chatty way to ask. The formal version is Qu'est-ce que c'est ? – both are worth knowing.
Miam, or miam-miam, is the French 'yum'. The m's are sounded, unlike many French final letters.
Du = some. English can say 'have ketchup', but French always needs du, de la or des before food like this.
Dis-lui = tell him (or her): lui means 'to him/to her'. Dire à quelqu'un de faire = to tell someone to do something.
Copier = to copy. French has no separate '-ing' form: il me copie means both 'he copies me' and 'he's copying me'.

phrases.fr: Il en a plus que moi !
phrases.note: Plus que = more than. After que, use moi, not je. The s of plus is usually sounded in 'more' comparisons.
Juste = fair here. In speech it's often squashed to C'est pas juste ! – the classic sibling complaint.
Végétarienne is the girl's form; a boy says végétarien. Maintenant (now) can also go first: Maintenant, je suis végétarienne.

phrases.en: Do I have to eat all of it?
phrases.note: Je dois = I have to, from devoir. Tout (everything) slips in before the infinitive: tout manger = eat it all.

phrases.fr: Juste un petit peu, s'il te plaît.
phrases.ph: zhewst-uhn puh-tee puh, seel tuh pleh
phrases.note: Un petit peu = a little bit. S'il te plaît is for one person you call tu; s'il vous plaît is the polite or plural version.

phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce qu'il y a comme dessert ?
phrases.note: Qu'est-ce qu'il y a comme ... ? = What is there for ...? Pudding is simply le dessert in French.

phrases.en: Can I have it with nothing on it?
phrases.fr: Je peux l'avoir sans rien dessus ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh la-vwar sahn ryan duh-sew
phrases.note: Sans rien = with nothing, and dessus = on top. For plain food you can also say nature: un yaourt nature.
Le collège is secondary school for ages 11–15 (le lycée comes after), not a college. C'était = it was.
La journée = the day as time you live through. Passée gets an extra e to match journée, which is feminine.

phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait aujourd'hui ?
phrases.note: Tu as fait = you did, from faire. Qu'est-ce que at the start turns it into a 'what' question.

phrases.fr: Il s'est passé quelque chose d'intéressant ?
phrases.ph: eel seh pa-say kel-kuh shohz dan-tay-reh-sahn
phrases.note: Quelque chose de + adjective = something ... . De shortens to d' before intéressant, and the adjective never changes.
Les devoirs (plural) = homework. Un devoir on its own is one assignment, or a duty.
Tes = your, for plural things; ton and ta are for single things. Faire ses devoirs = to do your homework.
Literally 'It's for when?' – the everyday way to ask about a deadline. Answer with C'est pour demain or C'est pour lundi.
L' = it (le shortened before a vowel). It sits in front of as, not after fini as in English.
Avoir besoin de = to need, literally 'to have need of'. De becomes d' before aide.

phrases.en: Have you got a test tomorrow?
phrases.note: Un contrôle = a class test. Un examen is a big official exam, like the brevet or the bac.
Réviser = to revise, just like in English. Tu as + révisé builds the past: have you revised.

phrases.en: What lesson have you got first?
phrases.fr: Tu as quel cours en premier ?
phrases.ph: tew a kel koor ahn pruh-myay
phrases.note: Un cours = a lesson. Quel matches cours, which is masculine; with a feminine noun it would be quelle.
À quelle heure ... ? = At what time ...? Tacking it on at the end, as here, is the chatty spoken order.

phrases.fr: Tu veux que je vienne te chercher ?
phrases.ph: tew vuh kuh zhuh vyen tuh shehr-shay
phrases.note: Venir chercher quelqu'un = to come and pick someone up. After tu veux que, venir takes the special form vienne.

phrases.en: Where should I pick you up?
phrases.note: Te (you) goes right before chercher. Leaving où (where) until the end is how people really talk at home.

phrases.en: What time should I pick you up?
phrases.fr: Je viens te chercher à quelle heure ?
phrases.ph: zhuh vyan tuh shehr-shay a kel-ur
phrases.note: Same frame as the 'where' question – just swap où for à quelle heure. Je viens here means 'shall I come'.

phrases.fr: Envoie-moi un texto quand tu as fini.
phrases.ph: ahn-vwa-mwa uhn tek-stoh kahn tew a fee-nee
phrases.note: Un texto (or un SMS) = a text. In a command, moi goes after the verb with a hyphen: envoie-moi = send me.

phrases.en: Let me know when you're ready.
phrases.note: Prête is for a girl – a boy is prêt. Dis-moi (tell me) comes from dire.

phrases.fr: N'oublie pas tes affaires de sport.
phrases.note: Tes affaires = your things or stuff, so affaires de sport = PE kit. Oublie is the tu command of oublier (to forget).
Préparer = to get something ready, so it covers 'pack'. Un sac is any bag; an old-style school satchel is un cartable.

phrases.en: Do you need anything for tomorrow?
phrases.fr: Tu as besoin de quelque chose pour demain ?
phrases.ph: tew a buh-zwan duh kel-kuh shohz poor duh-man
phrases.note: Quelque chose = something or anything, always two words. Pour demain = for tomorrow.
D'abord = first (of all). Fais is the command form of faire, used without tu.

phrases.en: What have you got to do?
phrases.note: Tu dois + infinitive = you have to ... . Dois comes from devoir – the same root as les devoirs.

phrases.fr: Ça s'est passé comment, le contrôle ?
phrases.ph: sa seh pa-say ko-mahn, luh kohn-trohl
phrases.note: Ça s'est passé = it went. Adding the thing at the end after a comma, le contrôle, is very typical spoken French.
Une note = a mark, not a written note. Tu as eu = you got, from avoir. French marks are usually out of 20.
Bravo works for any success. Bien joué ! (literally 'well played') is also really common between family and friends.

phrases.en: Who did you have lunch with?
phrases.fr: Tu as mangé avec qui à midi ?
phrases.ph: tew a mahn-zhay a-vek kee a mee-dee
phrases.note: À midi here means at lunchtime, not strictly 12 o'clock. Avec qui = with whom, happily left at the end in speech.
Copines = (girl) friends; for boys or a mixed group, say copains. Vont is from aller, used for how people are.

phrases.fr: Montre-moi ce que tu as fait.
phrases.ph: mohn-truh-mwa suh kuh tew a feh
phrases.note: Ce que = what, meaning 'the thing that'. Montre-moi = show me, from montrer.

phrases.en: Put your books in your bag.
phrases.fr: Range tes livres dans ton sac.
phrases.ph: rahnzh tay leevr dahn tohn sak
phrases.note: Ranger = to put away or tidy – you'll hear it constantly at home. Dans = in or into.

phrases.en: Don't leave it till the last minute.
phrases.note: Attendre = to wait for – no separate word for 'for'. Dernière is feminine to match la minute.
After a negative, des turns into de: j'ai des devoirs becomes je n'ai pas de devoirs.
Déjà = already, and it sits between ai and fait. L' is le (it) shortened before ai.
Je ferai is the future of faire (I will do). Plus tard = later – the classic teenage stalling line.

phrases.en: I need help with my homework.
phrases.fr: J'ai besoin d'aide pour mes devoirs.
phrases.ph: zhay buh-zwan ded poor may duh-vwar
phrases.note: French says help 'for' homework: de l'aide pour mes devoirs. Mes = my, for plural things.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Tu peux ... ? = Can you ...? Just add an infinitive: tu peux m'aider, tu peux venir. M' = me.
Ne ... pas wraps around the verb comprends (from comprendre). In fast speech the ne often disappears.
Vérifier = to check. For a quick look, regarder works too: Tu peux regarder ça ?
Imprimer = to print, and the printer is une imprimante. Je dois = I have to.
Marcher means to walk, but also 'to work' for machines. Ça ne marche pas = it doesn't work.

phrases.en: I need something for school tomorrow.
phrases.fr: J'ai besoin de quelque chose pour le collège demain.
phrases.ph: zhay buh-zwan duh kel-kuh shohz poor luh ko-lezh duh-man
phrases.note: Pour le collège = for school. Time words like demain usually go at the very end.
J'ai oublié = I forgot, from oublier. Add de + verb to say what: j'ai oublié de le faire.

phrases.fr: J'ai besoin d'argent pour le collège.
phrases.ph: zhay buh-zwan dar-zhahn poor luh ko-lezh
phrases.note: L'argent = money (it also means silver). After besoin de, it becomes d'argent.

phrases.en: I need you to sign this.
phrases.fr: Il faut que tu me signes ça.
phrases.ph: eel foh kuh tew muh seeny sa
phrases.note: Il faut que tu ... = you need to ... . The me means 'for me', which French likes to add.
Un contrôle = a test in class. To say what you're doing about it: je révise pour le contrôle.

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.fr: Je ne veux pas aller au collège.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh vuh pa a-lay oh ko-lezh
phrases.note: Au is à + le squashed together: aller au collège. Before a feminine word it stays à la: aller à la piscine.
Fatiguée is the girl's form; a boy says fatigué. Both sound exactly the same.
Ennuyeux = boring. Careful: to say you're bored, use je m'ennuie – je suis ennuyeuse means you're a boring person!
Ça allait = it was OK, the past of ça va. A classic shrug answer; C'était bien sounds a bit keener.
Ne ... rien = nothing. Rien slots in before passé, not after it.
Sais is from savoir, to know a fact. In casual speech the ne is often dropped: je sais pas.
Se souvenir de = to remember. En stands for 'of it', so it has to be there: je ne m'en souviens pas.
On = we in everyday French; nous is more formal. Don't forget the n' – it's easy to miss because it blends into on.
Venir chercher = to come and get, i.e. pick up. Me goes just before chercher.

phrases.en: Can you pick me up early?
phrases.fr: Tu peux venir me chercher plus tôt ?
phrases.ph: tew puh vuh-neer muh shehr-shay plew toh
phrases.note: Plus tôt = earlier, two words. Don't confuse it with plutôt, one word, which means rather.

phrases.en: What time are you picking me up?
phrases.fr: Tu viens me chercher à quelle heure ?
phrases.ph: tew vyan muh shehr-shay a kel-ur
phrases.note: Tu viens = you're coming. Like English, French uses the present tense for plans already made.
Interroger = to quiz someone on what they've learnt – it's what teachers do in class. Not the same as a police interrogation here!
C'est pour + day = it's due on that day. So C'est pour lundi = it's due Monday.
Note is feminine, so bon becomes bonne. A really good mark might be 17/20.
Réussir = to succeed or pass. False friend: passer un examen means to sit an exam, not to pass it.
Rater = to fail, and also to miss (rater le bus). It's the everyday word; échouer sounds more formal.
Je dois + infinitive = I've got to ... . Réviser needs no extra word: je dois réviser les maths.
Je peux ... ? = Can I ...? L'ordinateur is often shortened to l'ordi at home.
Être collé = to get a detention, literally 'to be glued'. Collée is for a girl; a boy says je suis collé.
Une sortie scolaire = a school day trip; un voyage scolaire usually means one with nights away.
Va + infinitive = go and ... . Va is the tu command of aller, and it has no s.

phrases.fr: C'est le bazar dans ta chambre.
phrases.ph: say luh ba-zar dahn ta shahnbr
phrases.note: Le bazar = a mess, a very common word at home. Une chambre is a bedroom; any room in general is une pièce.
Ta (not ton) because chambre is feminine: la chambre. Rangé is from ranger, to tidy.
Ramasser = to pick something up off the floor. Ça = that, used all the time in spoken French.
Range ça = put that away. The same verb, ranger, means to tidy a whole room.
Clothes are les vêtements, nearly always plural; un vêtement is a single item of clothing.

phrases.en: Put your dirty clothes in the wash.
phrases.fr: Mets tes vêtements sales dans le panier à linge.
phrases.ph: meh tay vet-mahn sal dahn luh pa-nyay a lanzh
phrases.note: Sales takes an s to match vêtements. Le panier à linge is the laundry basket – where dirty clothes go in a French home.
Propre = clean. Before a noun it means 'own' instead: ma propre chambre = my own room.

phrases.en: Don't leave it on the floor.
phrases.fr: Ne le laisse pas par terre.
phrases.ph: nuh luh les pa par tehr
phrases.note: Par terre = on the floor. Laisser = to leave something somewhere; to leave a place is partir.
Faire son lit = to make your bed, same idea as English. The t at the end of lit is silent.
Un rideau = a curtain. Words ending in -eau add x, not s, in the plural: rideaux.
Ouvrir is irregular, but its tu command, ouvre, ends in -e like an -er verb. Watch the circumflex in fenêtre.
Fermer = to close; ferme is the command. Its opposite gives ouvre la fenêtre.
La porte = the door. Don't mix it up with le port, which is a harbour.
Ouverte = open, feminine to match la porte. With le placard (cupboard) it would be ouvert.
Éteindre = to switch off, and also to put out a fire. Éteins is the tu command.
Allumer = to switch on or to light. The same verb works for la télé or une bougie (a candle).
Descendre = to go down, but with an object it means to bring something down. No word for 'stairs' needed.
Monter = to go up, or to take something up. Add là-haut (up there) if you want to be extra clear.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Aider à + verb says what the help is for: tu peux m'aider à porter ça ? = can you help me carry this?
Un coup de main = a hand (help), literally 'a hit of hand'. Donner un coup de main = to help out.
Être à quelqu'un = to belong to someone. So C'est à qui ? = Whose is it? – and the answer is C'est à moi.
À toi = yours, literally 'to you'. Swap the word: c'est à moi (mine), c'est à lui (his).
The same ça va as 'how are you?', but here aller keeps its real meaning: where does it go?

phrases.fr: Tu peux passer l'aspirateur dans ta chambre ?
phrases.ph: tew puh pa-say las-pee-ra-tur dahn ta shahnbr
phrases.note: Passer l'aspirateur = to hoover, literally 'to pass the vacuum'. Aspirateur comes from aspirer, to suck up.
Les draps = sheets. False friend: they're not drapes – curtains are les rideaux.
Une serviette = a towel, but at the table it's a napkin. Accrocher = to hang up.
Sortir = to go out, but with an object it means to take something out. La poubelle = the bin.

phrases.en: Can you hang the washing out?
phrases.note: Le linge = the washing or laundry. Étendre le linge = to hang it out to dry.
Rentrer = to come back in, but also to bring something inside – handy when it starts to rain.
Plier = to fold. Like all -er verbs, the tu command drops the s: tu plies becomes plie.
Sentir = to smell. Ça sent mauvais = it smells bad; ça sent bon = it smells nice.

phrases.en: There are dirty cups in your room.
phrases.fr: Il y a des tasses sales dans ta chambre.
phrases.ph: eel-ya day tas sal dahn ta shahnbr
phrases.note: Il y a = there is or there are – it never changes. Sale already ends in e, so with tasses it just adds s.
Le tour = turn. You can also say C'est pas à moi – c'est à moi de ... means it's my turn to ... .
Hier = yesterday. The h is silent, so the word starts with the vowel sound.
Très bien = perfectly fine here, not just 'very good'. Chambre is feminine, so later you'd say elle est bien.
Arrête de + verb = stop doing something. De shortens to d' before entrer.

phrases.fr: Ne touche pas à mes affaires !
phrases.note: Toucher à = to touch or mess with. Mes affaires = my stuff – a phrase teenagers use all the time.
Je le fais = I'll do it. French often uses the present for something happening soon.
Moi is the form of 'me' used on its own or after c'est. Toujours = always, but also still.
L' stands for la chambre, so rangée gets an extra e. It sounds the same, but it matters in writing.
Il est où ... ? is the relaxed spoken way to ask where something is. Il because aspirateur is masculine.

phrases.en: It's his turn to empty the dishwasher.
phrases.fr: C'est à lui de vider le lave-vaisselle.
phrases.ph: say-ta lwee duh vee-day luh lav-veh-sel
phrases.note: C'est à lui de + verb = it's his turn to ... . Lave-vaisselle breaks down as lave (washes) + vaisselle (dishes).
Comme ça = like this, that way. L' (it) comes before aime, just as with other verbs.

phrases.fr: Je sais où tout se trouve.
phrases.ph: zhuh seh oo too suh troov
phrases.note: Se trouver = to be (located), literally 'to find itself'. Où tout se trouve = where everything is.
Frapper = to knock (it also means to hit). Avant de + verb = before doing: avant d'entrer.
For a 'don't' command, put ne before the verb and pas after it. Range itself doesn't change.

phrases.en: Where did you put my hoodie?
phrases.fr: Tu as mis mon sweat où ?
phrases.ph: tew a mee mohn sweet oo
phrases.note: Un sweat = a sweatshirt or hoodie, borrowed from English. Mis is the past form of mettre, to put.

phrases.fr: Maintenant, je ne trouve plus rien.
phrases.ph: man-tuh-nahn, zhuh nuh troov plew ryan
phrases.note: Ne ... plus rien = nothing any more. French happily stacks plus and rien together.
When someone calls you, French says j'arrive (I'm arriving), not je viens. Bon = fine, OK, with a sigh.
Sale = dirty. False friend: a sale in the shops is les soldes.
Mon lit, because lit is masculine. Add déjà for 'already': j'ai déjà fait mon lit.

phrases.en: Why do I have to do everything?
phrases.fr: Pourquoi c'est moi qui dois tout faire ?
phrases.ph: poor-kwa say mwa kee dwa too fehr
phrases.note: C'est moi qui ... = it's me who ... – a handy way to stress who's doing it. Tout faire = do everything.

phrases.fr: « Plus tard », ça veut dire maintenant.
phrases.ph: plew tar, sa vuh deer man-tuh-nahn
phrases.note: Vouloir dire = to mean, literally 'to want to say'. French quotation marks are « », with spaces inside.

phrases.en: I don't care whose it is.
phrases.note: Peu importe = it doesn't matter, whatever. Follow it with a question word: peu importe qui, peu importe où.
Pas de + noun = no ...: pas de devoirs, pas de télé. De shortens to d' before excuses.
Bof is the French shrug word: 'meh, whatever'. French puts « » round quoted words, with a space inside each one.

phrases.en: Don't roll your eyes at me.
phrases.fr: Ne lève pas les yeux au ciel !
phrases.ph: nuh lev pa lay-zyuh oh syel
phrases.note: Lever les yeux au ciel = literally 'raise your eyes to the sky', which is how French says roll your eyes. Les yeux = the eyes; one eye is un œil.

phrases.fr: Parce que c'est moi qui le dis.
phrases.ph: pars-kuh say mwa kee luh dee
phrases.note: C'est moi qui... = 'it's me who...' and puts heavy stress on the speaker. Parce que = because; before a vowel it becomes parce qu'.

phrases.en: You said that an hour ago.
phrases.fr: Tu as dit ça il y a une heure.
phrases.ph: tew a dee sa eel-ya ew-nur
phrases.note: Il y a + a time = ago: il y a une heure = an hour ago, il y a deux jours = two days ago. Here il y a doesn't mean 'there is'.

phrases.fr: Je ne vais pas te le redemander.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh veh pa tuh luh ruh-duh-mahn-day
phrases.note: Redemander = demander (to ask) + re- (again). French adds re- to lots of verbs: refaire (redo), relire (reread).
Said by a parent, répondre on its own means to answer back or be cheeky, not just to reply. Ne ... pas wraps round the verb.
Jusqu'à = up to / until: jusqu'à demain = until tomorrow. The p in compte is silent.
Dans + a time = in (that much time from now): dans une minute, dans une heure. Tout de suite (straight away) would work here too.

phrases.en: You're not busy, you're on your phone.
phrases.fr: Tu n'es pas occupée, tu es sur ton portable.
phrases.ph: tew neh pa-zo-kew-pay, tew eh sewr tohn por-tabl
phrases.note: Occupée is for a girl; to a boy it's occupé. Être sur son portable = to be on your phone, just like English.

phrases.en: I don't care who did it.
phrases.note: Peu importe = 'it doesn't matter'. Handy pattern: peu importe qui (who), peu importe quand (when), peu importe où (where).

phrases.en: If you know, why haven't you done it?
phrases.fr: Si tu le sais, pourquoi tu ne l'as pas fait ?
phrases.ph: see tew luh seh, poor-kwa tew nuh la pa feh
phrases.note: In the ne ... pas past tense, ne ... pas goes round the little verb as: tu ne l'as pas fait. Le = it, and shortens to l' before as.

phrases.fr: Alors pourquoi ce n'est pas fait ?
phrases.ph: a-lor poor-kwa suh neh pa feh
phrases.note: Fait means both 'done' and 'made' – it comes from faire, which covers both. Alors here = 'so then'.
Literally 'well tried', from essayer (to try). Usually said with a smile when someone's excuse hasn't worked.
Souffler = to blow or huff. Arrête de + verb = stop doing something: arrête de crier, arrête de râler.

phrases.fr: On me l'a déjà faite, celle-là.
phrases.ph: ohn muh la day-zha fet, sel-la
phrases.note: An idiom: 'someone's already pulled that one on me'. Celle-là (that one) is feminine because it stands for l'excuse.
Raconter des histoires = to tell stories, meaning to make things up. After ne ... pas, des turns into de (d' before a vowel).
French 'looks for' excuses: chercher = to look for. Careful: faire des excuses means to apologise, not to make excuses.
Ferai is the future of faire (to do): je ferai = I will do. Plus tard = later, literally 'more late'.

phrases.en: I'll do it in a minute.
phrases.fr: Je le fais dans une minute.
phrases.note: French often uses the present for something about to happen: je le fais = I'm doing it / I'll do it. Le = it, placed before the verb.

phrases.en: I was going to do it!
phrases.note: J'allais + infinitive = I was going to. It's the past form of je vais faire (I'm going to do).
Savoir is for knowing facts (je sais); connaître is for knowing people or places (je connais Paris). The s in sais is silent.
Word order trap: me comes before le (l'), and both go before the verb. Déjà = already, and goes after as.
Entendre = to hear (not 'intend'). Talking to Mum you'd write entendue – it sounds exactly the same.

phrases.fr: Je suis en train de le faire !
phrases.ph: zhuh swee-zahn tran duh luh fehr
phrases.note: Être en train de + verb = to be in the middle of doing. It stresses 'right now', which French plain present can't.
Attendre = to wait (not to attend). Attends is for one person; to a group it's attendez.
Un instant = a moment. You can also hear Un instant ! on its own, e.g. on the phone.
French asks for 'two seconds' where English asks for one. The c in secondes sounds like a g.
Pourquoi = pour + quoi, literally 'for what'. The answer starts with parce que (because).

phrases.en: Why do I have to do it?
phrases.fr: Pourquoi c'est moi qui dois le faire ?
phrases.ph: poor-kwa say mwa kee dwa luh fehr
phrases.note: Dois comes from devoir = to have to. As a noun, les devoirs means homework – things you have to do.

phrases.fr: Pourquoi il ne peut pas le faire, lui ?
phrases.ph: poor-kwa eel nuh puh pa luh fehr, lwee
phrases.note: Adding lui at the end stresses 'him' – like saying 'why can't HE do it?'. Peut comes from pouvoir (can).
Être à moi = to belong to me. Useful: C'est à qui ? = Whose is it? C'est à toi ? = Is it yours?
Le (it) shortens to l' before ai. Ne ... pas sits round ai, not round fait.
French uses the present here: 'it isn't me!'. In quick speech you'll often hear C'est pas moi !, with the ne dropped.

phrases.fr: Ce n'est pas moi qui l'ai laissé là.
phrases.ph: suh neh pa mwa kee leh leh-say la
phrases.note: Là with an accent = there; la without one = the. Laisser = to leave something somewhere.
Ranger = to tidy or put away: ranger sa chambre = tidy your room. Rangerai is the future: I will tidy.

phrases.fr: Ma chambre n'est pas si mal que ça.
phrases.ph: ma shahnbr neh pa see mal kuh sa
phrases.note: Pas si ... que ça = 'not that ...': pas si difficile que ça = not that hard. Chambre = bedroom; a room in general is une pièce.
Le = it for a masculine thing (mon sac). For a feminine one (ma veste) say Je ne la trouve pas.
Se ranger = to be put away – literally 'where does this put itself away?'. Putting où at the end is normal in chat.

phrases.en: What do you want me to do?
phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu veux que je fasse ?
phrases.ph: kes-kuh tew vuh kuh zhuh fas
phrases.note: After tu veux que (you want me to), faire changes to fasse – a special form French uses after 'want someone to'.
Literally 'am I obliged?'. Obligée is for a girl – a boy says Je suis obligé ?
Hier = yesterday; avant-hier = the day before yesterday. The h in hier is silent.
Son means his or her – it matches tour (masculine), not the person. So C'est son tour works for a brother or a sister.
Le tour = the turn, but la tour = the tower (la tour Eiffel). The le/la changes the meaning.

phrases.fr: C'est toujours moi qui le fais.
phrases.ph: say too-zhoor mwa kee luh feh
phrases.note: Toujours = always, but also 'still' (il dort toujours = he's still asleep). Fais matches moi: moi qui fais.
Occupée ends in -e because the speaker is a girl; a boy writes occupé. Both sound the same.
Fini comes from finir (to finish). Same pattern for other -ir verbs: choisir → j'ai choisi.
Propre = clean when it comes after a word, but 'own' before one: ma propre chambre = my own room.
Je peux ... ? = Can I ...? Just raise your voice at the end to make it a question: Je peux sortir ?

phrases.en: What do I get for it?
phrases.note: En échange = in exchange, in return. Putting quoi late in the question is casual and cheeky – good for bargaining.
Faute = fault, but also mistake: une faute d'orthographe = a spelling mistake. Faute is feminine, so ma.
Poser = to put down. Un portable is a mobile phone; a laptop is un ordinateur portable.
Lâcher = to let go of, so 'let go of your phone'. A bit sharp – fine from a parent.

phrases.en: How long have you been on your phone?
phrases.fr: Ça fait combien de temps que tu es sur ton portable ?
phrases.ph: sa feh kohn-byan duh tahn kuh tew eh sewr tohn por-tabl
phrases.note: Ça fait ... que + present = have been doing: ça fait une heure que j'attends = I've been waiting an hour. French uses the present, not the past.
Baisser = to lower or turn down. Musique is feminine, so ta, not ton.
In a command, le (it) goes after the verb with a hyphen. Here le stands for le son (the sound).
Fort usually means strong, but for sound it means loud. Trop = too (much).
Un casque = headphones (the over-ear kind), and also a helmet. Earbuds are des écouteurs. Mets is from mettre (to put on).
La télé is short for la télévision, so it's feminine. Baisser works for the TV just like for music.
Regarder = to watch or look at – no extra word for 'at'. Qu'est-ce que = what, at the start of a question.
Jouer à is for games and sports (jouer au foot); jouer de is for instruments (jouer du piano). So à quoi = at what.
Parler à = to talk to. Putting à qui at the end is the everyday way; À qui tu parles ? is also fine.
Encore here = still; it can also mean again (encore une fois) or more (encore cinq minutes).
Il faut + verb = it needs to be done / you need to. French says recharger for phones, with the re-.
Chargeur ends in -eur, and most -eur words for gadgets are masculine: un chargeur, un ordinateur. So ton.

phrases.en: Don't forget to charge your phone.
phrases.fr: N'oublie pas de recharger ton portable.
phrases.ph: noo-blee pa duh ruh-shar-zhay tohn por-tabl
phrases.note: N'oublie pas de ... = Don't forget to ... Ne becomes n' before the vowel of oublie.

phrases.fr: Tu as passé assez de temps devant les écrans.
phrases.ph: tew a pa-say a-say duh tahn duh-vahn lay-zay-krahn
phrases.note: French says time 'in front of' screens: devant les écrans. Assez de = enough, with no le/la after it.
C'est l'heure de + verb = It's time to: c'est l'heure de manger. De becomes d' before arrêter.

phrases.fr: Encore cinq minutes, et après, tu arrêtes.
phrases.ph: ahn-kor sank mee-newt, ay a-preh, tew a-ret
phrases.note: Encore + a number = that many more: encore cinq minutes. Après = after, then.

phrases.en: No, I'm not extending your time limit.
phrases.fr: Non, je ne vais pas augmenter ta limite de temps.
phrases.ph: nohn, zhuh nuh veh pa ohg-mahn-tay ta lee-meet duh tahn
phrases.note: Augmenter = to increase. Limite is feminine, so ta limite, even though it ends like many masculine words.

phrases.en: Why do you need more time?
phrases.fr: Pourquoi tu as besoin de plus de temps ?
phrases.ph: poor-kwa tew a buh-zwan duh plews duh tahn
phrases.note: Avoir besoin de = to need, literally 'to have need of'. J'ai besoin de toi = I need you.
Reposer = to rest, from repos (rest). Don't mix it up with rester, which means to stay.
Éteindre = to switch off (and to put out a fire). The opposite is allumer: allume la télé = turn the TV on.
Télécommande = télé- (from a distance) + commande (control). Où with an accent = where; ou without one = or.
Écrire à = to write to, and French uses it for texting too. Écris is the tu form.
L'ordinateur = the computer; le shortens to l' before a vowel. In chat it's often shortened to l'ordi.

phrases.fr: Ce soir, tu laisses ton portable en bas.
phrases.ph: suh swar, tew les tohn por-tabl ahn ba
phrases.note: En bas = downstairs, en haut = upstairs. Ce soir = this evening / tonight.

phrases.en: Can you turn it up a bit?
phrases.fr: Tu peux monter un peu le son ?
phrases.ph: tew puh mohn-tay uhn puh luh sohn
phrases.note: Monter = to go up, and also to turn up the volume. Its opposite is baisser. Tu peux ... ? = Can you ...?

phrases.fr: Ne partage pas ça sur internet.
phrases.ph: nuh par-tazh pa sa sewr an-tehr-net
phrases.note: Partager = to share. Sur internet = online, literally 'on the internet'; en ligne also works.

phrases.en: Look at me, not your phone.
phrases.note: In a positive command, me turns into moi and goes after the verb with a hyphen: regarde-moi, aide-moi.
Very common spoken style: say il est où first, then name the thing. The textbook version is Où est mon portable ?
Vu is the past form of voir (to see): j'ai vu = I saw / I have seen.

phrases.fr: Tu peux faire sonner mon portable ?
phrases.ph: tew puh fehr so-nay mohn por-tabl
phrases.note: Faire + verb = to make something happen: faire sonner = make ring. Sonner = to ring.
À plat = flat – French phone batteries go flat too. Teens also say mon portable est mort (dead).
Où est ... ? = Where is ...? For more than one thing it becomes Où sont ... ? (où sont mes clés ?).
A statement becomes a question just by your voice rising. More formal: Est-ce que tu as vu mon chargeur ?
Emprunter = to borrow; prêter = to lend. So the other way round: Tu me prêtes ton chargeur ?

phrases.fr: C'est quoi, le mot de passe du wifi ?
phrases.ph: say kwa, luh moh duh pas dew wee-fee
phrases.note: Mot de passe = literally 'word of pass'. Du = de + le, because it's le wifi.
Marcher = to walk, but also to work for machines: ça marche ? = does it work? (also 'OK?').
Internet usually has no le in French. Lent = slow; the t is silent, but you hear it in the girl form lente.

phrases.en: Can you turn off the time limit?
phrases.fr: Tu peux enlever la limite de temps ?
phrases.ph: tew puh ahnl-vay la lee-meet duh tahn
phrases.note: Enlever = to take off or remove: enlève tes chaussures = take your shoes off.

phrases.fr: Je peux avoir plus de temps ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh a-vwar plews duh tahn
phrases.note: Plus de + noun = more ...: plus de temps, plus de frites. No le/la after de.
De plus after a number = more: deux jours de plus = two more days. Juste = just, as in English.
L' = le (it), shortened before as. Bloquer = to block, a handy near-copy of the English.

phrases.fr: J'en ai besoin pour le collège.
phrases.note: En means 'of it' here, since it's avoir besoin de. Careful: collège = secondary school (ages 11–15), not college.
Copines = friends who are girls. For boys, or a mixed group, it's copains. Mes works for both.
Presque = nearly, and slots between ai and fini. French says 'I have nearly finished'.

phrases.en: Wait, I'm just replying to someone.
phrases.note: Répondre à = to reply to. Quelqu'un = someone, from quelque (some) + un (one).

phrases.fr: Je n'ai presque plus de batterie.
phrases.ph: zhuh neh presk plew duh bat-ree
phrases.note: Ne ... plus = no more / not any longer. Add presque and it becomes 'hardly any left'.
Utiliser = to use. Je peux ... ? is the easy way to ask permission for almost anything.

phrases.fr: Tu peux me partager ta connexion ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh par-ta-zhay ta ko-nek-syohn
phrases.note: Hotspot on a French phone is called partage de connexion (sharing your connection) – that's where this comes from.
Données = data, literally 'given things'. Lots of French teens just say Je n'ai plus de data.
Fissuré = cracked; cassé = broken. Écran is masculine, so mon.
Appli is short for application, which is feminine – hence cette. Télécharger = to download.
Reçu comes from recevoir (to receive). The ç keeps the c soft before u.
Envoyer = to send; te (to you) shortens to t' before a vowel. Lien = link.
In France the home router is la box, as the internet company provides it. Redémarrer = to restart.
Lis is the tu command of lire (to read); the s is silent. To several people it would be Ne lisez pas.

phrases.en: Can you top up my phone?
phrases.note: Recharger = to top up (and to recharge). Most French teens have a monthly plan, called un forfait.
Embêter = to annoy or bother – everyday and not rude. De shortens to d' before embêter.
Laisser quelqu'un tranquille = to leave someone alone, literally 'leave them calm'. Laisse-moi tranquille ! = Leave me alone!
Arrêtez (not arrête) because it's said to two people. Se disputer = to argue with each other; vous is the 'each other' bit.
Tous les deux = both of you. For two girls it becomes toutes les deux; a boy and a girl take tous.
Se passer = to happen. Qu'est-ce qui (not que) because 'what' is the thing doing the happening.
Tu as fait covers both 'you did' and 'you have done' – French uses one past tense for both in speech.
Que shortens to qu' before il. Il a fait = he did / he has done.

phrases.fr: Ne rejette pas la faute sur lui.
phrases.ph: nuh ruh-zhet pa la foht sewr lwee
phrases.note: Rejeter la faute sur quelqu'un = literally 'throw the fault back onto someone', i.e. to blame them.
Rendre = to give back. Careful: rendre visite means to visit, not to give a visit back. Le = it, after the verb in a command.
À lui = his (belonging to him). The pattern works for everyone: à moi, à toi, à lui, à elle.
Son and sa don't show whether the owner is a boy or girl, so French uses à elle to make 'hers' clear.
Avant de + verb = before doing: avant de manger = before eating. Demander = to ask, not to demand.
Sois is the command form of être (to be). Gentille is for a girl; to a boy it's Sois gentil.
Chercher usually means to look for, but chercher quelqu'un means to wind someone up or pick a fight.

phrases.fr: Ne fais pas attention à lui.
phrases.note: Faire attention à = to pay attention to, so 'don't pay attention to him'. Ignore-le also works.
Literally 'let it fall' – the French way to say drop it or forget it. Very common with friends too.
From suffire = to be enough, so 'that is enough'. A firm way to end an argument.

phrases.en: I don't care who started it.
phrases.fr: Je me fiche de savoir qui a commencé.
phrases.ph: zhuh muh feesh duh sa-vwar kee a ko-mahn-say
phrases.note: Se ficher de = not to care about. Casual but not rude, so fine from a parent. Commencer = to start.
Réglez comes from régler (to sort out or settle). It's the vous form because you're telling both of them.
Excuse-toi comes from s'excuser (to apologise, literally 'to excuse yourself'). In a command, toi goes after the verb.
Laisse-le respirer means literally 'let him breathe a bit' – the French image for giving someone space.

phrases.en: Go away for five minutes and calm down.
phrases.ph: va-tahn sank mee-newt ay kalm twa
phrases.note: Va-t'en = go away. The t' is toi squashed before en. Calme-toi (calm yourself) also puts toi after the verb.
Arrête de + a verb = stop doing something. Swap crier (to shout) for any verb: arrête de râler (stop moaning).

phrases.en: Don't talk to him like that.
phrases.fr: Ne lui parle pas comme ça.
phrases.ph: nuh lwee parl pa kom sa
phrases.note: Lui = to him. You speak à someone in French (parler à), so 'him' becomes lui, not le.
Chacun son tour = literally 'each one his turn'. It's a set phrase, so no verb is needed.
Partagez is the vous command of partager (to share), because you're telling two people. To one person: partage.
Cafter is slang for telling tales or snitching. A kid who does it is un cafteur (boy) or une cafteuse (girl).

phrases.en: You're both as bad as each other.
phrases.fr: Vous êtes aussi pénibles l'un que l'autre.
phrases.ph: voo-zet oh-see pay-neebl luhn kuh lohtr
phrases.note: Aussi ... l'un que l'autre = as ... as each other. Pénibles (annoying) has an s because it describes both of you.
Gentiment = nicely. It comes from gentil (kind) – it doesn't mean 'gently', which is doucement.

phrases.en: Keep the noise down, you two.
phrases.note: Moins de bruit = literally 'less noise'. Vous deux = you two, the way to speak to a pair.

phrases.en: That's not how we talk to each other.
phrases.fr: On ne se parle pas comme ça.
phrases.ph: ohn nuh suh parl pa kom sa
phrases.note: Se parler = to talk to each other. At home, on nearly always means 'we', not 'one'.
C'est lui qui... = it's HIM who... A handy pattern for pointing the finger: c'est lui qui a cassé ça.
Chambre = bedroom, not 'chamber'. A room in general is une pièce.
Dis-lui de + a verb = tell him to... Dis is the command of dire (to say), and lui (to him) follows it.
Sors comes from sortir (to go out). Sortir de = to get out of, so 'out of my room' is de ma chambre.
Me (me) goes before the verb: me copier = to copy me. The same pattern gives arrête de me suivre (stop following me).
C'est à moi = it's mine, literally 'it's to me'. Swap the last word: c'est à toi (yours), c'est à lui (his).
Juste here means fair. In fast speech the ne often disappears: c'est pas juste !

phrases.fr: Il a toujours ce qu'il veut.
phrases.note: Ce qu'il veut = what he wants. Ce que (ce qu' before a vowel) means 'what' in the middle of a sentence.
Qu'est-ce qu'il est... ! = he's so...! Pénible means annoying or a pain – it doesn't mean 'painful'.
Teens use trop to mean 'so' or 'really', not just 'too'. Said to a girl it's énervante.
Tranquille = calm, in peace, so it's literally 'leave me in peace'. Moi goes after the verb in a command.
Embêter = to annoy or bother. M' (me) sits before the verb: il m'embête = he's bugging me.
Frappée has an extra e because a girl is speaking. A boy writes frappé – it sounds exactly the same.
In speech, là often means 'here', not just 'there'. En premier = first.
Rendre = to give back. In this command le (it) comes before moi, joined with hyphens.
Arrête = stop, said to one person. To two or more people it becomes arrêtez.
Dégage is blunt, like 'clear off!'. Fine between siblings, rude to anyone else – va-t'en is softer.
Regarder = to look at – the 'at' is built in, so no extra word. Me goes before the verb.

phrases.fr: Ne touche pas à mes affaires !
phrases.note: Affaires = your stuff or belongings. Toucher à means to touch or mess with something.
Ment comes from mentir (to lie), and its final t is silent. A liar is un menteur.
Tais-toi comes from se taire (to go quiet). Blunt but not swearing – fine for a brother, not for a teacher.
Tour here is masculine (le tour = turn), so it's mon tour. La tour means a tower!
Pris is the past form of prendre (to take). The m' shows who it was taken from: il m'a pris = he took from me.
Faire le bébé = to act like a baby. Bébé is always masculine, even for a girl: un bébé.
L' = him, placed before the verb. In the past tense ne ... pas wraps around ai: je ne l'ai pas touché.
Où with an accent means where. Without the accent, ou means 'or'.
Chien is masculine: le chien. A female dog is une chienne.
Tu as vu... ? = have you seen...? Just raise your voice at the end to turn it into a question.
Tu peux ... ? = can you ...? Faire sortir means to let or send someone out.
Rentrer = to come (back) in. Faire + a verb means to get someone – or a dog – to do it.
Sortir = to go out. It's the same verb for going out with friends: je sors ce soir.

phrases.en: Can you take Monty for a walk?
phrases.note: Promener = to walk (a dog). With se – se promener – it means going for a walk yourself.

phrases.en: Has Monty been for a walk?
phrases.note: Promenade = a walk. It's feminine, so it's sa promenade – and sa can mean his or her.

phrases.fr: On lui a donné à manger ?
phrases.ph: ohn lwee a do-nay a mahn-zhay
phrases.note: Donner à manger = to feed, literally 'to give to eat'. On here means 'someone' or 'we'.

phrases.fr: Tu peux donner à manger au chien ?
phrases.ph: tew puh do-nay a mahn-zhay oh shyan
phrases.note: Au = à + le. You give food to the dog, and à le always squashes into au.
De l'eau = some water. Eau is feminine, but before a vowel la shortens to l'.
Gamelle = a pet's bowl (it can also mean a lunchbox). Vide = empty.
Laisse = a dog's lead. Don't mix it up with laisse from laisser (to leave) – same spelling, different word.
Mets is the command of mettre (to put). Lui after it means 'on him'.
Laisser + a verb = to let someone do something. Le (him) goes just before laisse.
Portail = gate, and it's masculine: le portail. Ferme comes from fermer (to shut).
Appelle has a double l, from appeler (to call). The same verb gives je m'appelle – I'm called.
Canapé = sofa. Fais-le descendre = make him get down; du is de + le (off the).

phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce qu'il a dans la gueule ?
phrases.note: Gueule = an animal's mouth. Used about a person it's rude, so save it for the dog.
Enlever = to take away or off. Lui shows who you're taking it from: enlève-lui ça = take that off him.

phrases.fr: Arrête de lui donner à manger.
phrases.ph: a-ret duh lwee do-nay a mahn-zhay
phrases.note: Lui (to him) goes right before the verb it belongs to: lui donner = to give him.
Ne ... pas wraps around both lui and the verb: ne lui donne pas. Ça = that.
Faire pipi = to do a wee, the word you'd use with a child. Doit comes from devoir (must, have to).
Ramasser = to pick up. Crotte is the everyday, not-rude word for dog poo.
Sacs à crottes = poo bags. À shows what something is for, as in une tasse à café (a coffee cup).
Aboyer = to bark, and the y turns into i: il aboie. In speech, pourquoi is often followed by normal word order.

phrases.fr: Il a les pattes pleines de boue.
phrases.ph: ee-la lay pat plen duh boo
phrases.note: Pattes = an animal's paws or legs. Pleines ends in -es to match pattes, which is feminine and plural.
Essuyer = to wipe or dry. French says les pattes, not ses, because lui already shows whose paws.

phrases.en: Don't let him on the bed.
phrases.fr: Ne le laisse pas monter sur le lit.
phrases.ph: nuh luh lehs pa mohn-tay sewr luh lee
phrases.note: Monter sur = to climb onto. The t at the end of lit (bed) is silent.
Comprimé = a tablet (medicine). A tablet computer is une tablette – don't mix them up.
Assis is the standard dog command for 'sit', literally 'seated'. Couché means 'lie down'.
Friandise = a treat or sweet. It's feminine: une friandise.
Vomi is the past of vomir (to be sick). Don't use malade here – that means ill, not throwing up.

phrases.en: Can Monty sleep in my room?
phrases.fr: Monty peut dormir dans ma chambre ?
phrases.ph: mohn-tee puh dor-meer dahn ma shahnbr
phrases.note: Peut comes from pouvoir (can). Keep normal word order and raise your voice – no est-ce que needed.
Voler means both 'to steal' and 'to fly'. Il m'a volé = he stole from me.

phrases.en: Do I have to walk him?
phrases.note: Je dois = I have to. Le (him) goes before promener: le promener = to walk him.
Mignon = cute. For a girl or a female dog it becomes mignonne, with a double n and an e.
Puer = to stink – blunt, but not rude. The politer version is il sent mauvais (he smells bad).
Avoir besoin de = to need, literally 'to have need of'. De + un becomes d'un.
C'est qui ... ? = who's ...? This loose word order is typical of playful baby-talk with pets.

phrases.fr: Quelqu'un lui a donné à manger ?
phrases.ph: kel-kuhn lwee a do-nay a mahn-zhay
phrases.note: Quelqu'un = someone, or 'anyone' in a question: quelqu'un a vu mon portable ?
Encore means 'again' here, but it can also mean 'still'. The context tells you which.
Descends = get down, from descendre. It's also how you'd tell someone to come downstairs.
Assis is the dog's 'sit'. To tell a person to sit down you'd say assieds-toi.
Viens is the command form of venir (to come). At home you'll often hear viens là as well.
Lâche = drop it or let go, from lâcher. As a describing word, lâche means cowardly.
C'est bien = well done, literally 'it's good'. Mon chien sounds affectionate, like 'my boy'.
Lécher = to lick. The accent turns into è in il lèche, when the ending isn't pronounced.

phrases.fr: Il est encore sur mon lit.
phrases.note: Sur mon lit = on my bed. Dans mon lit would mean in it, under the covers.

phrases.en: Can I give him a treat?
phrases.fr: Je peux lui donner une friandise ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh lwee do-nay ewn free-ahn-deez
phrases.note: Je peux ... ? = can I ...? Add any verb: je peux sortir ? (can I go out?)

phrases.en: It's not my turn to walk him.
phrases.fr: Ce n'est pas à moi de le promener.
phrases.ph: suh neh pa a mwa duh luh prom-nay
phrases.note: C'est à moi de + a verb = it's my turn or my job to... Wrap it in ne ... pas to say it isn't.
Laisse ça = leave it, from laisser (to leave). Non works on French dogs just as 'no' does in English.
Putting où (where) at the end is very common in chat. Vas comes from aller (to go).
Y = there, so tu y vas = you're going there. Avec qui = with who.
Qui = who. Y stands in for the place, so you don't have to repeat it.

phrases.en: What are you going to do?
phrases.note: Aller + a verb = going to do something: tu vas faire, just like English 'going to'.
À quelle heure = at what time. Pars comes from partir (to leave).

phrases.en: What time will you be back?
