phrases.note: Rentrer = to come home. French often uses the present for soon: tu rentres = you'll be back.
Comment = how. To answer: en bus, en train, en voiture, or à pied (on foot).

phrases.fr: Tu as besoin qu'on te dépose ?
phrases.ph: tew a buh-zwan kohn tuh day-pohz
phrases.note: Déposer quelqu'un = to drop someone off – the usual way to offer a lift.

phrases.en: Do you want me to take you?
phrases.note: Tu veux que je... ? = do you want me to...? Emmener = to take someone somewhere.

phrases.fr: Il faut que je vienne te chercher ?
phrases.ph: eel foh kuh zhuh vyen tuh shehr-shay
phrases.note: Venir chercher = to pick someone up, literally 'come to fetch'. Il faut que = do I need to.

phrases.en: Message me when you get there.
phrases.fr: Envoie-moi un message quand tu arrives.
phrases.ph: ahn-vwa mwa uhn may-sazh kahn tew a-reev
phrases.note: Envoie comes from envoyer (to send). Un message and un texto both mean a text.

phrases.en: Let me know if your plans change.
phrases.ph: pray-vyan mwa see tay plahn shahnzh
phrases.note: False friend: prévenir means to let someone know or warn, not 'prevent' (that's empêcher).
Allumé = switched on, from allumer (which also means to light). Off is éteint.

phrases.en: Make sure your phone has some charge.
phrases.fr: Vérifie que ton portable est chargé.
phrases.ph: vay-ree-fee kuh tohn por-tabl ay shar-zhay
phrases.note: Vérifie que... = check that... – a handy start for any reminder. Chargé = charged.
Assez de = enough. Argent means money, as well as silver.
Manteau = coat, and it's masculine: ton manteau. A lighter jacket is une veste.
Prends is the command of prendre (to take) – the same verb as in prendre le bus.
Weather uses faire, not être: il fait froid = it's cold. Dehors = outside.
Il pleut comes from pleuvoir (to rain). Like English 'it rains', it only ever uses il.
Trop tard = too late. Here trop really does mean 'too'.
Fais attention = be careful, literally 'make attention'. Faire turns up in lots of set phrases like this.
Amuse-toi comes from s'amuser (to have fun, literally 'to amuse yourself'). Bien adds 'well'.
À tout à l'heure = see you later today. For a vaguer 'later' there's à plus tard, texted as À+.
Se retrouver = to meet up. It's vous because you mean the whole group.
Conduit comes from conduire (to drive). A driving licence is le permis.

phrases.en: Will there be an adult there?
phrases.note: Il y aura = there will be – the future of il y a (there is).
False friend: rester means to stay, not to rest. Restez is the vous form, for the group.

phrases.en: Don't go off on your own.
phrases.note: Toute seule is for a girl; a boy is tout seul. Toute adds 'all' – all on your own.
Clés = keys (sometimes spelt clefs). The s is silent, as in most plurals.
Si = if. After si, French uses the present tense just like English: si je t'appelle.
Rentrer à la maison = to go home. Directement = straight, a word you can guess from 'directly'.

phrases.en: I'll pick you up at ten.
phrases.fr: Je viens te chercher à dix heures.
phrases.ph: zhuh vyan tuh shehr-shay a dee-zur
phrases.note: Liaison trap: the x of dix links to heures with a z sound. You can't leave out heures in French.

phrases.en: Say hi to them from me.
phrases.ph: dee lur bohn-zhoor duh ma par
phrases.note: De ma part = from me. Leur = to them, and it goes after the verb in a command.
Sortir = to go out, including going out with friends. Add ce soir for 'tonight'.
On = we in everyday speech, and it takes the il form of the verb: on peut.
M' = me, and it sits before the verb. Emmener = to take someone somewhere.

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift?
phrases.note: Emmener = to take someone somewhere, here by car. Tu peux ... ? = Can you ...? — reuse it for any request.
French has no single verb for 'pick up' someone: venir chercher = come and get, literally 'come look for'.
Y means 'there' and sits before the verb, just after nous (us): nous y emmener = take us there.

phrases.en: Can you pick us up later?
phrases.fr: Tu peux venir nous chercher plus tard ?
phrases.ph: tew puh vuh-neer noo shehr-shay plew tar
phrases.note: Plus tard = later, literally 'more late'. Swap me for nous to turn 'pick me up' into 'pick us up'.
Amie with -e is a girl friend, yet it's mon, not ma, because amie starts with a vowel. For a boy: mon ami.

phrases.en: Can I have a friend over?
phrases.fr: Je peux inviter une copine à la maison ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh an-vee-tay ewn ko-peen a la may-zohn
phrases.note: Une copine = a (girl) friend; a boy is un copain. Careful: ma copine can also mean 'my girlfriend'.

phrases.fr: Elle peut venir à la maison ?
phrases.ph: el puh vuh-neer a la may-zohn
phrases.note: À la maison means 'home' or 'to ours' — no word for 'house' needed in English. For a boy, swap elle for il.
Rester is a false friend: it means to stay, not to rest. The next verb follows straight on: rester dîner.

phrases.fr: Elle peut dormir à la maison ce soir ?
phrases.ph: el puh dor-meer a la may-zohn suh swar
phrases.note: Ce soir = tonight (literally 'this evening'). French says 'sleep at the house' where English says 'stay over'.

phrases.en: Can I stay at her house?
phrases.note: Chez + a person = at their house: chez elle, chez moi, chez Mamie. No word for 'house' needed.
Rester dormir = stay and sleep, the everyday way to ask for a sleepover. Two verbs side by side, nothing between them.

phrases.en: What time do I have to be home?
phrases.fr: Je dois rentrer à quelle heure ?
phrases.note: Rentrer = to come back home. Putting à quelle heure (at what time) at the end is normal in chatty French.

phrases.en: Do I have to come home that early?
phrases.note: Si tôt = so early. Don't mix it up with aussitôt (straight away), which sounds the same.

phrases.fr: Tous les autres restent plus tard.
phrases.note: Tous les autres = all the others. Restent is 'they stay' — rester means to stay, not to rest.
Je t'envoie = I'll send you. French often uses the present tense for something you're about to do.
Tenir au courant = to keep someone informed, literally 'hold in the current'. It's like 'I'll keep you posted'.
En route = on the way — English borrowed it. Another favourite text: j'arrive (I'm coming).
On means 'we' in spoken French and takes the il/elle form of the verb: on part, never on partons.
Presque = nearly. Arrivés ends in -s because on means several people; a group of only girls writes arrivées.
In everyday speech là usually means 'here', not just 'there'. Keep the accent: la without it means 'the'.
Dehors = outside; its opposite is dedans (inside). The h in dehors is silent.
Tu es où ? is how people really ask on the phone. The textbook version, Où es-tu ?, means the same.

phrases.fr: Tu en as pour combien de temps ?
phrases.ph: tew ahn-na poor kohn-byan duh tahn
phrases.note: En avoir pour = to need (an amount of time). Combien de temps = how long, literally 'how much time'.
Se dépêcher = to hurry. The little word changes with the person: je me dépêche, tu te dépêches.

phrases.en: Can I go to the cinema?
phrases.note: Au is à + le squeezed together, so 'to the cinema' is au cinéma. Teens often shorten it to au ciné.

phrases.en: I'm going to my friend's house.
phrases.note: Chez = to/at someone's home, so 'house' disappears. Mon amie (girl) and mon ami (boy) sound exactly the same.
Se retrouver = to meet up, literally 'to find each other again'. En ville = in town.

phrases.en: Can I go to a party on Saturday?
phrases.fr: Je peux aller à une fête samedi ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh a-lay a ewn fet sam-dee
phrases.note: Samedi with no word in front = this Saturday. Le samedi would mean every Saturday. No 'on' needed.
Anniversaire = birthday (and anniversary). It's son even for 'her', because anniversaire is a masculine word.

phrases.fr: Ce soir, je reste à la maison.
phrases.ph: suh swar, zhuh rest a la may-zohn
phrases.note: Je reste à la maison = I'm staying home. French puts ce soir (tonight) first quite often, with a comma.

phrases.en: Her mum will bring me back.
phrases.note: Ramener = to bring someone back. Sa mère can mean 'her mum' or 'his mum' — sa matches mère, not the person.

phrases.en: Can I stay a bit longer?
phrases.fr: Je peux rester encore un peu ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh res-tay ahn-kor uhn puh
phrases.note: Encore un peu = a bit more, literally 'again a little'. Handy for bargaining: encore cinq minutes !
Avant = before. In dix heures the x links on and sounds like a z before heures.

phrases.en: Wait for me in the car.
phrases.note: Voiture (car) is feminine, so la voiture. Attendre already means 'wait for', so there's no word for 'for'.
Viens is the tu command of venir (to come). Talking to both kids at once? Venez ici.
Va-t'en comes from s'en aller (to go away). Blunt — fine at home when you're cross, rude to anyone else.
Attends is the command of attendre. Verbs ending in -re keep their silent -s in tu commands.
Là can mean here or there — in this order, pointing, it means 'there'. Stay put: reste là.
Écoute comes from écouter. Verbs ending in -er lose their -s in tu commands: tu écoutes → écoute.
Regarder already means 'to look at', so no extra word: regarde ça = look at that.
Arrête comes from arrêter (to stop). The ê marks an s that dropped out long ago — think 'arrest'.
French has no one-word 'Don't!'. A sharp non (no) does the same job — it's all in the tone.
Ne ... pas wraps round the verb to make it negative: fais ça (do that) → ne fais pas ça.
Laisser = to leave something where it is. Laisse ça = leave that alone; ça is everyday French for 'that'.
Poser = to put down or place. Pose ça = put that down. Poser une question means to ask a question.
In a command, le (it) goes before moi, all joined by hyphens. For a feminine thing, like la télécommande: donne-la-moi.
Apporter = to bring a thing. For bringing a person, French uses amener instead.
Tiens is what you say as you hand something over, like 'here you go'. It comes from tenir (to hold).
The moi means 'for me' — a chatty add-on. Tiens-moi ça = hold this for me.
Aider = to help. It takes the person straight after it: aide-moi, aide ton frère.
Attention on its own is the warning shout, like 'careful!'. Same spelling as English but said the French way.
Faire attention = to be careful, literally 'make attention'. Add à for what to watch: fais attention à la route.
Dépêche-toi is the command of se dépêcher (to hurry). In a command, toi goes after the verb with a hyphen.
Moins vite = less fast. You could also say ralentis, from ralentir (to slow down).
Se calmer = to calm down, literally 'to calm yourself'. Calme-toi is the command.
The -ment ending often matches English -ly: sérieusement = seriously, lentement = slowly.
Qu'est-ce que = what, before 'you do'. Faire means both 'to do' and 'to make'.
Tu as fait = you have done / you did. Fait is the past form of faire, built with avoir.
Pourquoi = why, literally 'for what'. The answer starts with parce que (because).
Comment = how. Said alone it can also mean 'sorry, what?' when you didn't hear.
The accent matters: où = where, but ou without it = or.
Quand = when. Its d is silent on its own but sounds like a t before a vowel: quand il part.
Qui = who. A dit = said, from dire (to say). Qui is never shortened to qu'.
Vouloir dire = to mean, literally 'to want to say'. Ça veut dire quoi ? = what does that mean?
Déjà = already. Te (to you) and l' (it) both squeeze in before ai: je te l'ai dit = I told you it.

phrases.fr: Je te l'ai demandé trois fois.
phrases.ph: zhuh tuh lay duh-mahn-day trwa fwa
phrases.note: Demander is a false friend: it means to ask, not demand. Fois = time as in 'three times'.
Pas on its own works as 'not': pas maintenant (not now), pas moi (not me), pas ce soir (not tonight).
Dans = in, for time counted from now: dans une minute, dans dix minutes. Minute is feminine, so une.
Plus tard = later. The s of plus is silent here, and so is the d of tard.
Peut-être = maybe, literally 'can be'. Keep the hyphen: without it, peut être just means 'can be'.
Verra is the future of voir (to see), so on verra = we'll see. The classic parent answer that often means no.
Hors de question = out of the question. Firm and final. The h of hors is silent.
D'accord = okay, fine — literally 'in agreement'. In texts it often shrinks to d'acc.
Vas-y = go on. The command va gets its s back before y so the two words flow together.
Ça suffit = that's enough, from suffire (to be enough). Said firmly, it ends the argument.
Regarde-moi = look at me. Moi goes after the verb with a hyphen, as in every positive command.
Tais-toi comes from se taire (to go quiet). It's blunt, close to 'shut up', so keep it for home.
Fort means strong but also loud: parle moins fort = speak less loudly; parle plus fort = speak up.
Répondre = to answer. The d and s in réponds are both silent, and the s stays in the command.

phrases.en: Don't talk to me like that.
phrases.fr: Ne me parle pas comme ça.
phrases.ph: nuh muh parl pa kom sa
phrases.note: Comme ça = like that. In a 'don't' command, me stays in front of the verb: ne me parle pas.
Plaisanter = to joke. Lots of people say je rigole pas, using the chattier verb rigoler.
Bien sûr = of course. Keep the circumflex: sur without it means 'on'.
Quoi on its own = what? It's a bit blunt with a parent — oui ? or pardon ? sounds nicer.
J'arrive = I'm coming, literally 'I'm arriving'. It's the automatic reply when someone calls you.
Deux secondes (two seconds) is the French 'hang on a sec'. The c in seconde sounds like a g.
Adding mais (but) turns a plain non into a protest, like 'no way!' or 'of course not!'
Moi = me when it stands alone. Je only works right before a verb, so never pourquoi je here.
Seconde is feminine, so it's une seconde. Teens also just say deux sec.
Pff is the French huff of annoyance. With d'accord (okay) it makes a very grudging yes.
Arrête ! = stop it! Aimed at your brother and a friend together, it becomes arrêtez !
Pousse-toi = move over, literally 'push yourself'. Blunt — fine with your brother, rude to anyone else.
Rendre = to give back. Rends-le-moi = give it back to me; for a feminine thing it's rends-la-moi.
Chut is the French 'shh'. Unusually, the final t is actually said.
Occupée has an extra -e because the speaker is a girl — a boy says occupé. It sounds the same either way.
Same words as a parent's order. To both parents at once it becomes dépêchez-vous !
Regarde ! is perfect for pointing things out. To more than one person: regardez !
Dégage ! = get lost! Much ruder than va-t'en — keep it for your brother, never for adults.
Bof is the French shrug word: not bothered, meh. Say it flatly for full teenage effect.
No verb and no ne needed: pas moi does the whole job. Same pattern: pas lui ! (not him!)
Literally 'it isn't me' — French uses the present here. In speech the ne often vanishes: c'est pas moi !
Attendre already means 'to wait for', so don't add pour. Attends-moi = wait for me.
Tranquille = calm, peaceful, so this is 'leave me in peace'. Cheeky with a parent, but not rude.
Ça va literally means 'it goes'. The reply can be the same two words: ça va (I'm fine).
Quoi de neuf = what's new. Neuf also means nine — the context tells you which.
Tu sais quoi ? = you know what? It comes from savoir (to know a fact) and is the classic way to start news.
Se passer = to go, for an event. Ça s'est bien passé ? = did it go well? Alors (so) opens the question.
Raconter = to tell what happened, like telling a story. Raconte ! on its own means 'go on, tell me'.
Ah bon ? reacts to news, like 'oh really?'. Bon normally means good, but not in this phrase.
Génial = brilliant. It's an adjective, so a feminine noun gives géniale: une idée géniale.
Works just like English. Add mince ! for a mild 'oh no, bother' that's safe to say anywhere.
Literally 'what isn't going?'. Another common way: qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? (what's the matter?)
C'était = it was, the past of c'est. Tacking qui (who) on the end is the normal chatty order.
Penser = to think. En here means 'about it', so tu en penses = you think about it.
Croire = to believe, and y stands for 'it'. Many people drop the ne: j'y crois pas !
Partir = to leave. Le travail = work; au boulot is the slangy version you'll hear a lot.
Je rentre = I'll be home, using the present. In six heures the x links on and sounds like a z.
Aimer means love or like. With a person, je t'aime is love; for friends say je t'aime bien (I like you).
Tu fais quoi = what are you doing. Quoi at the end is the relaxed version of qu'est-ce que tu fais.
La journée = the day, as in all day long, so ta journée. Passée takes -e to agree with feminine journée.
Ça va ? with your voice going up = are you okay? The answer can be the same words, said flat: ça va.
Crevé = shattered, an informal word for very tired. Mum would say crevée; the neutral word is fatigué.
Quel/quelle = what a... in exclamations. It's quelle here because journée is feminine.
Rentré = back home. Mum would write rentrée — it sounds identical, the extra e is just for a woman.
S'inquiéter = to worry, literally 'to worry yourself'. Friends shorten it to t'inquiète.
Tout = everything. Say it without the question voice and tout va bien means 'all good'.
Fier = proud; a mum says fière. After de, 'you' is toi, not te.

phrases.en: Did you have a good time?
phrases.note: S'amuser = to have fun, literally 'to amuse yourself'. Amusée has an extra e for a girl; to a boy say amusé.
Papa has no accent in French, unlike Spanish papá. Mon père is the more formal 'my father'.
Maman is what French children call their mum at any age; ma mère is 'my mother' when talking about her.
Quoi ? is the everyday 'What?' but can sound blunt. Pardon ? is politer when you just didn't hear.
Qu'est-ce que = what (literally 'what is it that'). Fais comes from faire, which means both 'to do' and 'to make'.
Spoken French often puts où (where) at the end: Tu es où ? The textbook version is Où es-tu ?
Vas comes from aller (to go): je vais, tu vas, il va. Où with an accent means where; ou without it means 'or'.
Où est ... ? = Where is ...? Swap in any person or thing: Où est mon portable ?
No le or la before Papa: family names like Papa and Maman behave like first names.
You'll also hear Il est où, Monty ? A male dog is il (he), never 'it'.
Il here means 'it', not 'he'. Heure is feminine, so it's quelle. Casual version: Il est quelle heure ?
On is everyday French for 'we'. Jour is masculine, so quel, not quelle. Answer: On est lundi.
À quelle heure ... ? = At what time ...? Partir means to leave, so on part = we're leaving.
Aujourd'hui = today, one word with an apostrophe inside. Qu'on is que + on squashed together.
Quelque part = somewhere or anywhere, written as two words. On va = we're going.
Y aller = to go (there). French needs the little y; On peut aller on its own sounds unfinished.
Prêt is for a man or boy, like Dad. Asking Mum, add an e: Tu es prête ?

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.fr: Tu en as pour combien de temps ?
phrases.ph: tew ahn-na poor kohn-byan duh tahn
phrases.note: Tu en as pour ... is an idiom for 'it'll take you ...'. Combien de temps = how much time.
Viens voir = come and see. French puts the two verbs side by side with no word for 'and'.
Regarder = to look at, with the 'at' built in, so never add à. Ça = this or that.
Regarder covers both 'look' and 'watch'. Bien here means 'closely' rather than 'well'.
Écouter = to listen to, no extra word for 'to'. Don't mix it up with entendre, which means to hear.
Devine comes from deviner (to guess). Another favourite opener: Tu sais quoi ? (You know what?)

phrases.fr: Tu sais ce qui s'est passé ?
phrases.ph: tew say suh kee say pa-say
phrases.note: Se passer = to happen, so s'est passé = happened. Ce qui means 'what' when it's the subject of the verb.

phrases.fr: Tu ne devineras jamais ce qui s'est passé.
phrases.ph: tew nuh duh-veen-ra zha-meh suh kee say pa-say
phrases.note: Ne ... jamais = never; the two words wrap round the verb. Devineras is the future form of deviner (to guess).
Drôle = funny (it can also mean odd). C'est marrant is just as common and a bit more casual.
Bizarre is spelt as in English and means weird or odd. C'est étrange is a slightly more serious alternative.
Énervant = annoying, from énerver (to get on someone's nerves). It doesn't mean 'unnerving'.
Dégoûtant = disgusting; keep the hat on the û. Teens also just say Beurk ! (Yuck!)
La honte = shame, and C'est la honte ! is the teen way to say 'How embarrassing!'. The h blocks the apostrophe: la honte, never l'honte.
Juste means fair here. In speech the ne often disappears: C'est pas juste !
Je m'en fiche = I don't care, casual and a bit cheeky. Je m'en fous is much ruder, so skip that one with parents.
Ne ... pas wraps round sais to make it negative. In speech the ne often vanishes: Je sais pas.
Peut-être = maybe, literally 'can be'. Keep the hyphen: peut être without it means 'can be'.
Sûrement looks like 'surely' but usually means 'probably'. Probablement works too.
D'accord = fine/OK, literally 'in agreement'. Friends shorten it to D'acc.
Ça marche = OK, that works, literally 'that walks'. French people use OK on its own too.
Peu importe = whatever, literally 'little matters'. Said with a sigh, it's just as dismissive as in English.
Sérieux ? is the casual teen version of Sérieusement ? Same meaning, more attitude.
Vrai = true, so C'est vrai ? is literally 'Is it true?'. You can also say Vraiment ?
Pas possible ! is Ce n'est pas possible with the start chopped off, short and punchy for 'No way!'.
Évidemment = obviously. French keeps the accent even on a capital É.
The ending -ment often works like English '-ly': exactement, rapidement, lentement.
Sais comes from savoir, to know a fact. For knowing a person or place, use connaître instead.
Arrête comes from arrêter (to stop). To more than one person, say Arrêtez !
Laisse-moi = leave me; tranquille = in peace. In a command, moi goes after the verb with a hyphen.
Va-t'en = go away, from s'en aller. Blunt: fine with a sibling, rude to anyone else.
Pénible = annoying or a pain, and it's the same for a man or a woman. Spoken quickly: T'es pénible.
Qu'est-ce que tu es ... ! = You're so ...! It looks like a question but it's an exclamation, so it ends in !
Merci = thanks. For 'thanks a lot' say merci beaucoup, never très merci.

phrases.fr: Pardon, je ne l'ai pas fait exprès.
phrases.ph: par-dohn, zhuh nuh lay pa feh eks-preh
phrases.note: Exprès = on purpose, so je ne l'ai pas fait exprès = I didn't do it on purpose. The final s is silent.
Je t'aime = I love you. Adding bien weakens it: Je t'aime bien only means 'I like you'.
S'ennuyer = to be bored, literally 'to bore yourself'. Don't say Je suis ennuyeuse, which means 'I'm boring'!
French teens use cool just like English. Trop bien ! (literally 'too good') is another favourite.

phrases.fr: Ce n'est pas grave, ne t'inquiète pas.
phrases.ph: suh nay pa grav, nuh tan-kyet pa
phrases.note: Pas grave = no big deal. Grave means serious here, nothing to do with a grave.

phrases.fr: Je peux te demander quelque chose ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh tuh duh-mahn-day kel-kuh shohz
phrases.note: Demander = to ask, not 'demand' (a false friend). Je peux ... ? = Can I ...? works with any verb.
Rigoler = to laugh or mess about, so Je rigole = I'm only joking. Also: C'est pour rire.
Rentrée is for a girl; a boy says Je suis rentré. Rentrer (to come home) uses être, not avoir, in the past.
Moi aussi = me too. For 'me neither', switch to moi non plus.
Ça va ? = Are you OK? The usual answer is the same two words, Ça va, meaning 'I'm fine'.
Literally 'what isn't going?'. A shorter, equally common option: Qu'est-ce que tu as ?
Avoir l'air = to look or seem. Contrariée ends in -ée for a girl; to a boy say contrarié.

phrases.fr: Tu ne te sens pas bien ?
phrases.ph: tew nuh tuh sahn pa byan
phrases.note: Se sentir = to feel, literally 'to feel yourself'. Te is the 'yourself' bit and sits before the verb.
Un pansement = a plaster for a cut. Avoid plâtre, which is a plaster cast. Avoir besoin de = to need.

phrases.fr: Où est-ce que tu as mal ?
phrases.note: Avoir mal = to hurt, literally 'to have bad'. Où est-ce que just turns it into a 'where' question.

phrases.en: Do you want to talk about it?
phrases.note: En means 'about it' and sits just before parler. Tu veux ... ? = Do you want to ...?
Comes from s'inquiéter (to worry). Casual French shortens it right down to T'inquiète !

phrases.en: Try not to stress about your exams.
phrases.fr: Essaie de ne pas stresser pour tes examens.
phrases.ph: eh-seh duh nuh pa streh-say poor tay-zeg-za-man
phrases.note: Essayer de = to try to. Before an infinitive (the 'to' form), ne pas stays together: ne pas stresser.
Se reposer = to rest. False friend alert: rester means to stay. Tu devrais = you should.
Fatiguée has an extra e for a girl; to a boy it's fatigué. Both sound exactly the same.
Mieux = better when describing how you feel or do something. Meilleur is for things: un meilleur film.
Grognon = grumpy, linked to grogner (to grunt or growl). It's normally used unchanged for girls and boys.
Souris is the command form of sourire (to smile). Same spelling as une souris, a mouse!
Literally 'stop your cinema'. A classic French telling-off for making a big fuss.
Du = some. Many French families just say Doliprane, the best-known paracetamol brand in France.

phrases.en: Do you need to see the doctor?
phrases.fr: Tu as besoin d'aller chez le médecin ?
phrases.ph: tew a buh-zwan da-lay shay luh mayd-san
phrases.note: Chez = at or to someone's place, so chez le médecin = to the doctor's. Médecin is the everyday word for a GP.

phrases.fr: Il s'est passé quelque chose au collège ?
phrases.ph: eel say pa-say kel-kuh shohz oh ko-lezh
phrases.note: Collège is secondary school for ages 11 to 15, not college. After that comes the lycée.

phrases.en: Go and lie down for a bit.
phrases.note: S'allonger = to lie down, literally 'to lengthen yourself'. Un peu = a bit.
Brûlante is for a girl; to a boy say brûlant. It comes from brûler, to burn.
Bu is the past form of boire (to drink). Assez de = enough, and de shrinks to d' before eau.

phrases.en: It's not the end of the world.
phrases.fr: Ce n'est pas la fin du monde.
phrases.ph: suh nay pa la fan dew mohnd
phrases.note: Du is de + le merged into one word: la fin du monde = the end of the world.

phrases.fr: Je ne me sens pas bien.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh muh sahn pa byan
phrases.note: Me ('myself') stays glued to the verb, so ne ... pas goes around both: ne me sens pas.
J'ai mal à ... = my ... hurts. Tête is feminine, so it's à la tête.
Ventre (tummy) is masculine, and à + le always merges into au: mal au ventre.
Gorge = throat, not a valley. It's feminine, so à la gorge.

phrases.en: I think I've got a temperature.
phrases.fr: Je crois que j'ai de la fièvre.
phrases.ph: zhuh krwa kuh zhay duh la fyevr
phrases.note: French says 'I have some fever': de la fièvre. Je crois que = I think that.

phrases.fr: Je suis inquiète pour mes examens.
phrases.note: Inquiète is the girl's form, with an è; a boy says inquiet, with a silent t.

phrases.fr: Je suis stressée par mes examens.
phrases.note: Stressée gets -ée for a girl; a boy says stressé. Mes examens = my exams (plural, so mes).
Un câlin = a hug or cuddle. To give one: faire un câlin.
J'en ai marre = I'm fed up, very common and casual. Add de for what: J'en ai marre des devoirs.
French uses aller (to go) for health: je vais bien = I'm well. The shorter reply is just Ça va.
Fiche-moi la paix = leave me in peace, but stronger than Laisse-moi tranquille. Cheeky, so family only.
Personne ... ne = nobody. Here personne doesn't mean 'a person' but 'no one'.
Avoir envie de = to feel like. You'll also hear J'ai mal au cœur, which means feeling sick, not heartache.

phrases.fr: J'ai la tête qui va exploser.
phrases.ph: zhay la tet kee va eks-ploh-zay
phrases.note: Literally 'I've got the head that's going to explode'. French uses la, not ma, for your own body parts.

phrases.fr: J'ai mal au ventre, j'ai mes règles.
phrases.ph: zhay mal oh vahntr, zhay may regl
phrases.note: Avoir ses règles = to have your period. Règles also means 'rules', but context makes it clear.
Trop really means 'too much', but teens use it for 'so' or 'really'. A boy says trop stressé.
À mourir = to death, so it's 'I'm bored to death'. A handy add-on for exaggerating.
Humeur (mood) is feminine, hence mauvaise. The opposite is de bonne humeur.
J'ai envie de + verb = I feel like doing something. Juste = just, only.
Literally 'I'm dying of hunger'. Plain hunger is J'ai faim ('I have hunger'), never je suis faim.
D'humeur = in the mood. Add à + verb to say for what: Je ne suis pas d'humeur à rire.

phrases.en: It's been the worst day ever.
phrases.fr: C'était la pire journée de ma vie.
phrases.ph: say-teh la peer zhoor-nay duh ma vee
phrases.note: Pire = worst. Journée is the day as a stretch of time you live through, which is why it's used instead of jour.
Crevée = shattered, casual; it literally means 'burst', like a tyre. A boy says crevé.
Exagérer has only one g, unlike English 'exaggerate'. The ne shortens to n' before the vowel.

phrases.en: I don't want to talk about it.
phrases.fr: Je ne veux pas en parler.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh vuh pa ahn par-lay
phrases.note: Veux comes from vouloir (to want): je veux, tu veux. Firm but not rude, so fine to say to a parent.

phrases.en: I think I'm getting a cold.
phrases.note: S'enrhumer = to catch a cold, from un rhume (a cold). French uses the present tense here for 'I'm getting'.
Fier is Dad's version. Mum adds an e and an accent: Je suis fière de toi.
Lâcher = to let go, so Ne lâche rien ! is literally 'don't let go of anything'. Big in French sport.
Y arriver = to manage it. The tiny y stands for 'it' here and is easy to miss.
Chance is feminine, so it's bonne, not bon. In French chance usually means luck.
Rendre bien = to turn out well, used about drawings, cakes or outfits. Super = really, in casual speech.
Aide is feminine, but French uses ton, not ta, before a vowel sound, so it's easier to say.
Fort normally means strong; here it's 'lots'. A warm family way to say it, often at bedtime or on the phone.
Jolie = pretty or lovely, for a girl. To a boy, Tu es très beau sounds more natural.
Continue comme ça = carry on like that. Tu commands of -er verbs drop the s: continue, not continues.

phrases.en: It doesn't matter if you get it wrong.
phrases.fr: Ce n'est pas grave si tu te trompes.
phrases.ph: suh nay pa grav see tew tuh trohnp
phrases.note: Se tromper = to make a mistake. Without the se, tromper means to trick someone.
De ton mieux = your best. Change the word for the person: je fais de mon mieux = I'm doing my best.

phrases.fr: Tu es vraiment douée pour ça.
phrases.ph: tew ay vreh-mahn doo-ay poor sa
phrases.note: Doué pour = good at, gifted at. Douée has the extra e for a girl; a boy is doué.
Félicitations is always plural, just like 'congratulations', and has only one accent, on the first é.
Gentille = kind (gentil for a boy). False friend: it doesn't mean gentle. Trop here means 'so'.
Bravo is the go-to French praise, for anything from a goal to a good mark.

phrases.en: I knew you could do it.
phrases.fr: Je savais que tu en étais capable.
phrases.ph: zhuh sa-veh kuh tew ahn-nay-teh ka-pabl
phrases.note: Être capable de = to be able to; en stands in for 'of doing it'. Savais = knew, from savoir.
Une note = a mark; French schools mark out of 20. Quelle is feminine to match note.
In this past form, little words like vraiment and beaucoup slot in between as and travaillé.
Génial = brilliant. It comes from génie (genius), so it's stronger than just bien.

phrases.fr: Tant pis, ce sera pour la prochaine fois.
phrases.ph: tahn pee, suh suh-ra poor la pro-shen fwa
phrases.note: Tant pis = never mind / too bad. Its opposite is tant mieux (so much the better). Ce sera is the future of c'est.
S'en sortir = to manage or get through something. Sortie ends in -e because the speaker is a girl; a boy says sorti.
Réussir = to succeed or manage. You'll also see réussir un examen = to pass an exam, which is very handy for GCSE.
Meilleure is 'best' for a woman, so this is said to Mum. To Dad it's Tu es le meilleur ! In speech, tu es often shrinks to t'es.
Note = mark or grade, not a written note. French uses avoir (j'ai eu = I got) for getting a mark.
Être doué(e) pour = to be good at, literally 'gifted for'. Douée is the girl's form; a boy says doué.
Maman takes a capital when used as a name, like Mum. Merci on its own is enough — no need for 'you'.
Word by word: I you it had said. The l' means 'it', and avais dit (had said) points back to earlier.

phrases.fr: Je suis trop fière de moi.
phrases.ph: zhuh swee troh fyehr duh mwa
phrases.note: Fière is 'proud' for a girl; a boy says fier. Trop normally means 'too', but teens use it for 'so' or 'really'.
Génial means brilliant or amazing, not 'genial'. One of the most useful positive words for speaking exams.
Bravo is the everyday French for 'well done' — you'll hear it from teachers too. Papa gets a capital as a name.
Pas mal drops the ne and c'est — the full version is Ce n'est pas mal. Often means 'pretty good', not just OK.
Assurer here is slang for 'to do brilliantly', not 'to assure'. You can praise someone with Tu as assuré !
French schools mark out of 20, so vingt sur vingt (20/20) is top marks. Anything over 10 counts as a pass.
Être reçu(e) = to pass an exam. Careful: passer un examen only means to sit it. A boy says Je suis reçu.
Trop cool is pure teen French — trop (really) plus the borrowed English cool. Keep it for friends and family.
S'il te plaît is literally 'if it pleases you'. Use s'il vous plaît to a teacher or to several people.
Dis is the command form of dire (to say) for one person. For more than one, it's Dites merci.
Literally 'what does one say?' — the classic parent prompt. On (one) is used all the time in French to mean 'we' or 'you'.
De rien = 'of nothing', like 'it's nothing'. Don't translate 'welcome' with bienvenue — that's only for greeting guests.
Souci = worry. After pas, du/des/une become de, which is why it's pas de souci. You'll also hear pas de problème.
Said after a sneeze: literally 'to your wishes'. To an adult you don't know well, say À vos souhaits !
Pardon is the quick, everyday way to say excuse me or sorry. The final n is not pronounced like in English.
Frapper = to knock (also to hit). French says 'before to enter': avant de + infinitive, so avant d'entrer.
Impoli = rude, the opposite of poli (polite). Rude in French (rude) means harsh or tough, so it's a false friend.
Ma chérie is 'my love' to a girl. For a boy it's mon chéri — the extra -e shows up in spelling only.
Couper la parole = to interrupt, literally 'to cut the speech'. Interrompre exists but sounds much more formal.
Ton frère = your brother; for a sister it would be ta sœur. Dire pardon à quelqu'un = to say sorry to someone.

phrases.en: Say it like you mean it.
phrases.fr: Dis-le comme si tu le pensais.
phrases.ph: dee-luh kom see tew luh pahn-seh
phrases.note: In a command, le (it) goes after the verb with a hyphen: dis-le. Comme si (as if) is followed by the imperfect, pensais.

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.fr: Ne parle pas la bouche pleine.
phrases.ph: nuh parl pa la boosh plen
phrases.note: French says 'the mouth full', not 'your mouth' — body parts usually take la/le. Pleine agrees with bouche (feminine).

phrases.en: Don't speak to me like that.
phrases.fr: Ne me parle pas comme ça.
phrases.ph: nuh muh parl pa kom sa
phrases.note: In a 'don't' command, me stays before the verb: ne me parle pas. In a positive one it moves after: parle-moi.
Literally 'change tone'. Ton is both 'tone' and 'your', so listen for context. A firm parent warning.
Mamie is the everyday word for grandma, and Papi for grandad. The formal words are grand-mère and grand-père.
Literally 'and politeness?' — a short French telling-off. Politesse = manners; poli means polite.
Use s'il te plaît with family and friends (tu). With teachers or several people it's s'il vous plaît.
Merci covers thanks and thank you. Careful: Non merci means no thanks, and merci alone can also mean no when offered something.
Beaucoup = a lot or very much. Never say très merci — beaucoup is the only word that goes with merci here.
Désolée ends in -e for a girl; a boy writes désolé. Both sound the same. Pardon works too for small things.

phrases.en: Excuse me, can I get past?
phrases.note: Je peux ... ? = Can I ...? — just add a verb in the infinitive. Passer here means to get past, not to pass an exam.
Merci pour = thanks for. Dîner is the evening meal; in France le déjeuner is lunch and le petit-déjeuner breakfast.
Je t'aime = I you love: t' (you) goes before the verb. Aimer means both to love and to like.
Moi aussi = me too, placed at the front for emphasis. You can also answer just Moi aussi !
Short for Ne t'inquiète pas (don't worry), from s'inquiéter = to worry. Very common in speech; write the full form in exams.
C'est bon ? here means 'Happy now?' — a grudging apology. Tone warning: it sounds sulky, which is the point.
J'ai dit is the perfect tense of dire (to say) — its past participle dit is irregular, so learn it by heart.

phrases.en: Sorry, can I just say something?
phrases.fr: Pardon, je peux juste dire un truc ?
phrases.ph: par-dohn, zhuh puh zhewst deer uhn trewk
phrases.note: Un truc = a thing or something, very common in speech. In writing, use quelque chose instead.
D'abord = first. It pairs with ensuite (then) and enfin (finally) — useful linking words for exam writing.

phrases.en: Sorry, I didn't do it on purpose.
phrases.fr: Pardon, je ne l'ai pas fait exprès.
phrases.ph: par-dohn, zhuh nuh lay pa feh eks-preh
phrases.note: Faire exprès = to do on purpose. Exprès is a false friend: it doesn't mean express. Note ne ... pas wraps round l'ai.
Couper la parole à quelqu'un = to interrupt someone. M' (me) comes before as, the helper verb, in the perfect tense.
Merci de + avoir + past participle = thanks for having done. Emmenée has an extra -e for a girl; a boy says emmené.

phrases.en: Can I leave the table, please?
phrases.fr: Je peux sortir de table, s'il te plaît ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh sor-teer duh tabl, seel tuh pleh
phrases.note: Sortir de table is the set phrase for leaving the table — no la needed. Quitter la table also works.

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.fr: Tu peux me donner un coup de main ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh do-nay uhn koo duh man
phrases.note: Un coup de main = a hand (help), literally 'a blow of hand'. Tu peux ... ? = Can you ...? — a pattern worth reusing.
Les courses = the shopping (always plural here). Aider quelqu'un à faire = to help someone do — note the à.

phrases.fr: Tu peux me tenir la porte ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh tuh-neer la port
phrases.note: Tenir = to hold. The me means 'for me', so word by word it's 'you can me hold the door?'
Aller ouvrir = to go and open (the door). French doesn't need to say 'the door' here — it's clear when the bell rings.
Avoir besoin de = to need, literally 'to have need of'. Aide is feminine: l'aide.
The present tense can make an offer: Je t'aide ? = Shall I help you? Te becomes t' before a vowel.
Laisse = leave it. Je vais + infinitive (I'm going to do) is the easy near future — very useful in exams.
Donne-moi = give me. In a command, me changes to moi and goes after the verb with a hyphen. Ça = that.
Montrer = to show, not 'to monitor'. Like donne-moi, the moi follows the verb in a command.
Attraper = to catch or grab. The moi here means 'for me', a handy way to ask someone to fetch something.
Passe-moi ... = pass me ... Use it at the table too: Passe-moi le sel (pass me the salt).
Literally 'what is it that isn't going?' — from aller (to go), as in Ça va ? You can also say Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?

phrases.fr: Je ne trouve pas mes lunettes.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh troov pa may lew-net
phrases.note: Lunettes (glasses) is always plural, so it's mes. French just says 'I don't find', with no word for 'can'.
Vu is the past participle of voir (to see). Clé (key) is feminine; you may also see it spelt clef, which sounds the same.
Regarder sur Internet = to look it up online. French doesn't capture 'look up' in one verb, so it names where to look.
Le (it) sits right before the verb it belongs to: à le trouver. Careful — à le doesn't merge into au before a verb.

phrases.en: Can you set this up for me?
phrases.note: Configurer = to set up a phone, app or computer. The me means 'for me'. For a device, installer is also common.

phrases.en: I could do with some help here.
phrases.fr: Un petit coup de main ne serait pas de refus.
phrases.ph: uhn puh-tee koo duh man nuh suh-reh pa duh ruh-few
phrases.note: Ne serait pas de refus = wouldn't be refused — a polite, slightly jokey hint. Serait is the conditional (would be) of être.
Me becomes m' before a vowel: m'aider. Say it all as one flowing word: tu peux m'aider.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: French often uses pour (for) where English says 'with' here. Aider avec ça is heard too, but pour ça sounds more natural.

phrases.en: Can you do this for me?
phrases.fr: Tu peux faire ça pour moi ?
phrases.ph: tew puh fehr sa poor mwa
phrases.note: After pour, use moi, not me: pour moi, avec moi, sans moi. Faire = to do or make.
Ouvrir = to open; its opposite is fermer (to close). The s of peux is silent, even before ouvrir.
Arriver à faire = to manage to do. Word by word: you manage to it grab? It's a very common way to say 'can you'.
Réparer = to fix or repair. Something that's fixed is réparé; something broken is cassé.
Regarder already means 'to look at', so don't add a word for 'at'. Same with écouter (to listen to).
Vérifier = to check. Handy for homework: Tu peux vérifier mes devoirs ? (Can you check my homework?)
Literally 'how does one do?' On is the everyday 'we/you/one'. A quick way to ask how anything works.
Vouloir dire = to mean, literally 'to want to say'. Great for class: Ça veut dire quoi en anglais ?
Se ranger = to be put away (literally 'to tidy itself'). Où (where) keeps its accent; ou without it means 'or'.
Here me goes before the infinitive montrer, not after it. Compare the command Montre-moi (show me).
Venir = to come. French doesn't need 'here' — venir already means towards the speaker. Add ici if you want to.
Tenir = to hold. It's irregular: je tiens, tu tiens, il tient — the same pattern as venir.
Porter = to carry, and also to wear (clothes). Context tells you which one.

phrases.en: Can you get this for me?
phrases.fr: Tu peux aller me chercher ça ?
phrases.ph: tew puh a-lay muh shehr-shay sa
phrases.note: Aller chercher = to go and get, to fetch. Chercher on its own means to look for, not 'to search' in the police sense.
Le = it (for a masculine thing); for a feminine thing it's la. It goes just before trouver (to find).
L' = it, squeezed before as. If 'it' is a feminine thing, the spelling becomes vue, though it sounds the same.

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.fr: Tu me donnes un coup de main ?
phrases.ph: tew muh don uhn koo duh man
phrases.note: Using the present tense (tu me donnes) instead of tu peux makes the request sound casual and friendly.
Coincé = stuck or jammed. It also describes a person who is uptight: il est coincé.
Cassé comes from casser (to break). Se casser la jambe = to break your leg.
Marcher = to walk, but also to work (for machines). Ça marche ! on its own means 'OK, deal!'
Y arriver = to manage it. The little y means 'it' or 'there'. Je ne peux pas would sound like you're not allowed.
Re- at the start of a verb means 'again': réexpliquer, relire, refaire. Me le = it to me.
Se faire mal = to hurt yourself. Reflexive verbs use être in the past: je me suis. Où ? Je me suis fait mal au genou.

phrases.fr: Je me suis coupé le doigt.
phrases.ph: zhuh muh swee koo-pay luh dwa
phrases.note: French says 'I cut myself the finger' — le doigt, not mon doigt. Coupé has no extra -e here, even for a girl.

phrases.fr: Tu peux me prêter le tien ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh preh-tay luh tyan
phrases.note: Prêter = to lend; emprunter = to borrow. Le tien = yours for a masculine thing; for a feminine one say la tienne.

phrases.en: I don't know how it works.
phrases.fr: Je ne sais pas comment ça marche.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh say pa ko-mahn sa marsh
phrases.note: Savoir = to know a fact or how to do something. In speech this is often shortened to Je sais pas.
Trop = too. Lourd = heavy; its opposite is léger (light). The d of lourd is silent.

phrases.fr: L'argent ne pousse pas sur les arbres.
phrases.ph: lar-zhahn nuh poos pa sewr lay-zarbr
phrases.note: Argent = money (and silver). Pousser = to grow here, though it also means to push. Watch the liaison: the s of les links onto arbres.

phrases.en: What do you need it for?
phrases.fr: Tu en as besoin pour quoi ?
phrases.note: En replaces 'of it', because avoir besoin de takes de. Pour quoi (for what) is not the same as pourquoi (why).
Cher = expensive, and also dear (as in Cher Paul). Its opposite is pas cher, which French uses for 'cheap'.
Combien = how much or how many. The shop-counter version is Ça coûte combien ?
Payer = to pay; paie is the command form. Avec ton argent = with your money; argent is masculine, so it takes ton.

phrases.en: You've already spent your pocket money.
phrases.fr: Tu as déjà dépensé ton argent de poche.
phrases.ph: tew a day-zha day-pahn-say tohn-nar-zhahn duh posh
phrases.note: Argent de poche = pocket money, word for word. Dépenser = to spend money; for time you use passer.
La moitié = half (as a noun). French often uses the present tense (je te donne) for a promise about now.

phrases.en: Put it on your birthday list.
phrases.note: Anniversaire = birthday, though it also means anniversary. Demande-le = ask for it; demander already includes 'for'.
Watch the n' — on and n'achète sound almost the same, so it's easy to forget when writing. On = we in everyday French.
Monnaie = change (coins), not 'money'. False friend: money is argent. Changer only means to exchange.

phrases.fr: C'est de l'argent jeté par les fenêtres.
phrases.ph: say duh lar-zhahn zhuh-tay par lay fuh-netr
phrases.note: Literally 'money thrown out of the windows' — a vivid French way to say wasted. Gaspiller = to waste.
Te l' = it to you — te always comes before le/l'. Envoyer = to send.

phrases.fr: Non, tu n'en as pas besoin.
phrases.note: N'en: the ne shortens to n' before en (of it). Ne ... pas goes round the whole en as.

phrases.en: What happened to your birthday money?
phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait de l'argent de ton anniversaire ?
phrases.ph: kes-kuh tew a feh duh lar-zhahn duh tohn-na-nee-vehr-sehr
phrases.note: Faire quelque chose de = to do something with, so literally 'what have you done with the money?'
Économiser = to save money. Sauver is only for saving a life. Tu vas devoir = you're going to have to.

phrases.en: Do I look like a bank?
phrases.fr: Tu me prends pour une banque ?
phrases.ph: tew muh prahn poor ewn bahnk
phrases.note: Prendre quelqu'un pour = to take someone for, i.e. mistake them for. Sarcastic — a classic parent line.
Ce ... -ci = this, pointing to now: ce mois-ci, cette semaine-ci. Mois keeps its s even in the singular.

phrases.en: You'll have to pay me back.
phrases.note: Rembourser = to pay back or refund. Devras is the future of devoir (to have to).
Les soldes = the sales, always plural. Attendre already means 'to wait for', so no word for 'for' is needed.

phrases.en: Do you think I'm made of money?
phrases.fr: Tu crois que je roule sur l'or ?
phrases.ph: tew krwa kuh zhuh rool sewr lor
phrases.note: Rouler sur l'or = to be rolling in money, literally 'to roll on gold'. L'or = gold.

phrases.fr: Tu peux me donner de l'argent ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh do-nay duh lar-zhahn
phrases.note: De l'argent = some money. French needs de l' where English can drop 'some'. French asks 'can you give me' rather than 'can I have'.

phrases.en: Can you send me some money?
phrases.note: M'envoyer = send me — me shrinks to m' before the vowel. Handy by text too.

phrases.fr: Tu peux me prêter de l'argent ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh preh-tay duh lar-zhahn
phrases.note: French flips it round: 'can you lend me' (prêter). Emprunter = to borrow, as in Je peux emprunter ton vélo ?
Rembourserai is the future tense: take the infinitive rembourser and add -ai. Te = you, placed before the verb.
Acheter = to buy. It gets a grave accent in some forms: j'achète, tu achètes. Ça is the everyday word for 'this/that'.

phrases.en: Can you buy this for me?
phrases.note: M' here means 'for me' — French doesn't need pour moi. So m'acheter = buy for me.
Commander = to order (food or online shopping). Quelque chose = something, written as two words.
Carte is feminine, so ta carte. Carte bancaire is a bank card; carte on its own can also mean a map or a menu.
Coûter = to cost, so this is literally 'it costs how much?'. In chatty French, combien (how much) often goes at the end.

phrases.fr: Ça ne coûte que cinq livres.
phrases.ph: sa nuh koot kuh sank leevr
phrases.note: Ne ... que means 'only' here, not 'not'. Une livre = a pound (money), but un livre = a book.
En promo is short for en promotion = on special offer. Les soldes are the big seasonal sales.
Avoir besoin de = to need (literally 'to have need of'). En stands in for 'of it', so J'en ai besoin = I have need of it.

phrases.fr: Tout le monde en a un.
phrases.note: Tout le monde = everyone, literally 'all the world'. It takes a singular verb: tout le monde a, never ont.

phrases.fr: On peut aller faire les magasins ?
phrases.ph: ohn puh a-lay fehr lay ma-ga-zan
phrases.note: Faire les magasins = to go round the shops for fun. Faire les courses is the food or everyday shopping.
On peut ... ? = Can we ...? On is the everyday word for 'we'. En ville = into town.

phrases.en: Can you take me to the shops?
phrases.fr: Tu peux m'emmener faire les magasins ?
phrases.ph: tew puh mahm-nay fehr lay ma-ga-zan
phrases.note: Emmener = to take a person somewhere. Me shortens to m' before a vowel, so m'emmener = take me.

phrases.en: I don't have any money left.
phrases.fr: Il ne me reste plus d'argent.
phrases.ph: eel nuh muh rest plew dar-zhahn
phrases.note: Il me reste = I have left (literally 'it remains to me'). After ne ... plus (no more), de l'argent becomes just d'argent.

phrases.en: Can I have my pocket money?
phrases.fr: Je peux avoir mon argent de poche ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh a-vwar mohn-nar-zhahn duh posh
phrases.note: Argent de poche is word for word 'money of pocket'. Argent also means silver.
Économiser = to save money. Saving a file on a computer is a different verb: enregistrer.
Trop = too (much). Cher means expensive, and it's the same word as 'dear' at the top of a letter: Cher Papa.

phrases.fr: Ça ne coûte vraiment pas cher.
phrases.ph: sa nuh koot vray-mahn pa shehr
phrases.note: French usually says 'not expensive' (pas cher) for cheap. Bon marché also means cheap and its ending never changes.

phrases.en: I want to buy her a present.
phrases.fr: Je veux lui acheter un cadeau.
phrases.ph: zhuh vuh lwee ash-tay uhn ka-doh
phrases.note: Lui = to her, but also to him, so context tells you who. It goes just before acheter (to buy).

phrases.en: Can I use my birthday money?
phrases.fr: Je peux utiliser l'argent de mon anniversaire ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh ew-tee-lee-zay lar-zhahn duh mohn-na-nee-vehr-sehr
phrases.note: L'argent de mon anniversaire is literally 'the money of my birthday'. French links nouns with de instead of stacking them like English.
Dépenser is only for spending money. For spending time, use passer: j'ai passé une heure. Tout sits between ai and dépensé.

phrases.en: Can you lend me ten pounds?
phrases.fr: Tu peux me prêter dix livres ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh preh-tay dee leevr
phrases.note: Prêter = to lend, emprunter = to borrow, and they're easy to mix up. Me prêter = lend me.
Vaut comes from valoir (to be worth). Un coup is usually a hit or blow, but ça vaut le coup is a fixed phrase: learn it whole.
La monnaie = the change (coins you get back). Money in general is l'argent, so don't mix them up.
Mets is the command form of mettre (to put on). La ceinture means belt; the full name is la ceinture de sécurité.

phrases.fr: Arrête de donner des coups de pied dans le siège.
phrases.ph: a-ret duh do-nay day koo duh pyay dahn luh syezh
phrases.note: Arrête de + verb = stop doing something. Un coup de pied = a kick, literally 'a blow of foot'.
Ranger = to put away or tidy up. It's the same verb as in Range ta chambre ! (Tidy your room!).
Presque = nearly, almost. The French say 'we are almost arrived' rather than 'almost there'.

phrases.fr: Il n'y en a plus pour longtemps.
phrases.note: Literally 'there isn't any more for long'. Ne ... plus = no longer; learn this one as a whole phrase for journeys and waiting.

phrases.en: Go to the toilet before we leave.
phrases.fr: Va aux toilettes avant qu'on parte.
phrases.ph: va oh twa-let a-vahn kohn part
phrases.note: Les toilettes is always plural, even for one toilet. Parte is a special form of partir (to leave) needed after avant que.
Faites is the vous command of faire, because the parent is talking to more than one child. Moins de bruit = less noise.
Essayer de + verb = to try to do something. Se concentrer is literally 'to concentrate yourself', so with je it becomes me concentrer.
Distraire = to distract. In a 'don't' command, ne ... pas wraps round the verb and me stays in front of it.

phrases.en: Who's in charge of the music?
phrases.note: S'occuper de = to be in charge of or look after. Qui s'occupe de ... ? works for any job: Qui s'occupe du chien ?
Pas encore usually means 'not yet', but said with a groan it means 'not ... again'. Cette is used because la chanson is feminine.

phrases.fr: Prends tes affaires, on est arrivés.
phrases.note: Tes affaires = your stuff, your things. Une bonne affaire, though, is a bargain.
Je t'attends is literally 'I wait for you'. Attendre already means 'wait for', so there's no extra word for 'for'.

phrases.en: Are you getting out or not?
phrases.note: Sounds impatient, which is the point. Descendre means to go down, and it's also the verb for getting out of a car or bus.
Monter = to go up, and also to get into a car, bus or train. Monte is the tu command, said to one person.

phrases.en: Hurry up, I'm in the car.
phrases.fr: Dépêche-toi, je suis dans la voiture.
phrases.ph: day-pesh-twa, zhuh swee dahn la vwa-tewr
phrases.note: Dépêche-toi comes from se dépêcher (to hurry). In a command, toi goes after the verb, joined by a hyphen.

phrases.fr: Arrêtez de vous disputer à l'arrière.
phrases.ph: a-reh-tay duh voo dees-pew-tay a la-ryehr
phrases.note: Se disputer = to argue with each other. Arrêtez and vous are plural because the parent is telling off both kids in the back.

phrases.fr: Ne mange pas dans la voiture.
phrases.ph: nuh mahnzh pa dahn la vwa-tewr
phrases.note: La voiture = the car. Watch out: the French word car means 'because' (and un car is a coach).

phrases.en: If you feel sick, tell me.
phrases.fr: Si tu as mal au cœur, dis-le-moi.
phrases.ph: see tew a ma-loh kur, dee-luh-mwa
phrases.note: Avoir mal au cœur = to feel sick, even though cœur means heart. Dis-le-moi is literally 'tell it to me'.
Par la fenêtre = out of (or through) the window. Par often means 'through' or 'by way of'.
Déposer quelqu'un = to drop someone off. French often uses the present tense (je te dépose) for something about to happen.

phrases.fr: Baisse un peu, s'il te plaît.
phrases.note: Baisser = to lower or turn down. S'il te plaît is for someone you call tu; to several people or a stranger, say s'il vous plaît.
Arriver uses être, not avoir, to talk about the past: on est arrivés. The s is there because on means several of us.
Il reste = there is ... left, from rester. False friend: rester means to stay or remain, never to rest.

phrases.fr: On va mettre combien de temps ?
phrases.ph: ohn va metr kohn-byan duh tahn
phrases.note: Mettre du temps = to take time. Mettre normally means 'to put', so learn this use as a set phrase.
Où with an accent means where; ou without one means or. That little grave accent changes the whole question.

phrases.en: Can I sit in the front?
phrases.note: Devant = in front, derrière = behind. S'asseoir = to sit down, literally 'to seat yourself', so je peux m'asseoir.

phrases.en: Can you turn the music up?
phrases.note: Monter le son = turn up the volume, literally 'raise the sound'. Le son means the sound, not the song (la chanson).
Le = it, and it goes before the verb: le baisser = turn it down. Here le stands for le son (the sound).
Je peux ... ? = Can I ...? Just add a verb in its dictionary form, like choisir (to choose), and you can ask for almost anything.
Quelque part = somewhere, literally 'some place'. S'arrêter is to stop yourself; arrêter on its own means to stop something.
Aux = à + les, which always merge. So 'to the toilets' is aux toilettes, never à les toilettes.
French says 'I have hunger' with avoir. Never say je suis faim, a very common mistake.
Literally 'I have thirst'. Like j'ai faim, it uses avoir (to have), not être (to be).
Fatiguée ends in -e because the speaker is a girl. A boy says je suis fatigué, which sounds exactly the same.
J'ai froid = I feel cold (literally 'I have cold'). Je suis froid would mean you're a cold, unfriendly person!
Use avoir for feeling hot. Je suis chaud is slang for something quite different, so avoid it here.

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating on?
phrases.note: Mettre means to put, but also to switch on: mettre le chauffage, mettre la télé. Le chauffage = the heating.

phrases.en: Can you turn the air conditioning on?
phrases.note: La climatisation is feminine, like nearly every French word ending in -tion.
Ouvrir = to open, fermer = to close. The ê in fenêtre often marks an old lost s, as in forêt (forest).

phrases.fr: On peut rentrer à la maison maintenant ?
phrases.ph: ohn puh rahn-tray a la may-zohn mant-nahn
phrases.note: Rentrer = to go back home. À la maison means both 'at home' and 'home' after a verb of movement.
The usual way to say you feel car-sick. The œ is o and e joined together, as in sœur (sister).
Recharger = to charge a battery. Charger alone usually means to load something up.

phrases.en: Can I put my headphones in?
phrases.note: Les écouteurs = earphones, from écouter (to listen). Big over-ear headphones are un casque, which also means a helmet.

phrases.fr: Il donne des coups de pied dans mon siège.
phrases.ph: eel don day koo duh pyay dahn mohn syezh
phrases.note: Mon siège uses mon because le siège (the seat) is masculine. Il donne is present tense, covering 'he's kicking'.

phrases.fr: Il y a beaucoup de circulation ?
phrases.note: La circulation = traffic. After beaucoup de (lots of), drop the le or la: beaucoup de circulation.
Putting où at the end is how people really talk. In writing you'd see the more formal Où sommes-nous ?

phrases.en: Can you pass me my bag?
phrases.fr: Tu peux me passer mon sac ?
phrases.ph: tew puh muh pa-say mohn sak
phrases.note: Passer = to pass or hand over. Me = to me, and it goes before the verb: me passer.
Vient comes from venir (to come), which is irregular: je viens, tu viens, il vient.
Blunt, but fine in a panic. Regarder already means 'look at', so there's no extra word for 'at'.
Literally 'there is some sun'. Many other weather phrases use il fait instead, like il fait beau (it's nice).

phrases.fr: Il fait un froid de canard.
phrases.note: Un froid de canard = freezing cold, literally 'a duck's cold'. It's an idiom, so don't try to translate it word for word.
Parapluie = para (against) + pluie (rain). Prends is the tu command of prendre (to take).

phrases.fr: Il y a vraiment beaucoup de vent.
phrases.note: French says 'there's wind' (il y a du vent) rather than 'it's windy'. Le vent = the wind.
De la = some, before a feminine noun like la crème. Solaire means 'of the sun', as in le système solaire.
Il va + verb = it's going to. Pleuvoir (to rain) only ever works with il: il pleut, il va pleuvoir.
Se couvrir = to cover yourself up. Bien adds 'properly', so couvre-toi bien = wrap up well.
Il fait chaud describes the weather. Compare j'ai chaud, which is how you personally feel.

phrases.fr: Il y a du verglas dehors.
phrases.note: Le verglas = black ice on roads and pavements. Dehors = outside; dedans = inside.
French has no '-ing' form, so il neige covers both 'it snows' and 'it's snowing'.

phrases.fr: Il y a un orage qui arrive.
phrases.note: Un orage is a thunderstorm; une tempête is a storm with strong winds. Qui arrive = that's on its way.

phrases.en: Bring the washing in, it's raining.
phrases.note: Le linge = the washing on the line. Rentrer usually means to go back in, but here it means to bring something in.
Où est ... ? = Where is ...? Handy for anything lost. Le manteau is masculine, so it's ton manteau.
Mettre = to put on clothes. Mets is said to one person; to several, it's mettez vos manteaux.

phrases.en: You're not going out like that, it's freezing.
phrases.fr: Tu ne sors pas comme ça, il gèle.
phrases.ph: tew nuh sor pa kom sa, eel zhel
phrases.note: Il gèle = it's freezing, from geler (to freeze). Comme ça = like that, a phrase you'll hear constantly.
Enlève comes from enlever = to take off (clothes, shoes). Its opposite is mettre (to put on).

phrases.en: Shut the door, you're letting the cold in.
phrases.fr: Ferme la porte, tu fais entrer le froid.
phrases.ph: fehrm la port, tew feh ahn-tray luh frwa
phrases.note: Faire entrer = to let in, literally 'make come in'. Faire + another verb means making something happen.

phrases.en: It's only a bit of rain.
phrases.fr: Ce n'est qu'un peu de pluie.
phrases.ph: suh neh kuhn puh duh plwee
phrases.note: Ne ... que = only, so ce n'est qu'un peu = it's only a little. La pluie is the rain; the verb is pleuvoir.

phrases.fr: Bois de l'eau, il fait chaud.
phrases.ph: bwa duh loh, eel feh shoh
phrases.note: Bois is the tu command of boire (to drink). De l' = some, used before a vowel: de l'eau.
Attraper froid = to catch a cold, literally 'catch cold'. The illness itself is un rhume.
Same words as 'it's going to rain'. Only your voice rising at the end turns it into a question.
Le temps means both 'weather' and 'time'. This is a classic GCSE question, so it's worth knowing by heart.
De shortens to d' before a vowel, so besoin de + un manteau becomes besoin d'un manteau.
Tremper = to soak or dip (like dipping a croissant in hot chocolate). Trempée is for a girl; a boy says trempé.
Quelle ... ! = What a ...! It has the -le ending because la chaleur (the heat) is feminine.
Literally 'I'm dying of cold', a dramatic but everyday exaggeration. Meurs comes from the irregular verb mourir (to die).

phrases.en: What's the weather going to be like tomorrow?
phrases.fr: Il va faire quel temps demain ?
phrases.ph: eel va fehr kel tahn duh-man
phrases.note: Il va faire + weather word = it's going to be: il va faire beau, il va faire froid.
On gèle = we're freezing, literally 'we freeze'. On is the everyday word for 'we', even when you're moaning.

phrases.fr: Je ne mets pas de manteau.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh meh pa duh mahn-toh
phrases.note: After ne ... pas, un changes to de: je mets un manteau, but je ne mets pas de manteau.
Crever de chaud = to be boiling. Crever (to burst, to die) is very informal: fine at home, not with teachers.
Trempé gets -es to match les chaussures, which is feminine and plural. You can't hear it, but you must write it.

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating up?
phrases.note: Le chauffage comes from chauffer (to heat). Monter is the everyday verb for turning anything up.
With likes and hates, French keeps le or la: je déteste la pluie, j'adore le soleil.

phrases.en: Can we go to the beach?
phrases.fr: On peut aller à la plage ?
phrases.ph: ohn puh a-lay a la plazh
phrases.note: À la = to the, before a feminine noun like la plage. With a masculine noun, à le always becomes au: au parc.
La neige is the snow and il neige is 'it's snowing'. They sound the same, so listen for il.
Ne and pas sit either side of the verb. Ne shortens to n' before a vowel: je n'ai pas.

phrases.en: Can you put the air con on?
phrases.note: La clim is short for la climatisation. Everyday French loves chopping long words: la télé, le frigo, le resto.
Encore = again here, though it can also mean 'still' or 'more'. Pff is the classic French sigh of annoyance.
Décoiffée = with messy hair, from coiffer (to do someone's hair). Toute décoiffée is for a girl; a boy says tout décoiffé.

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift? It's pouring.
phrases.fr: Tu peux m'emmener en voiture ? Il pleut à verse.
phrases.ph: tew puh mahm-nay ahn vwa-tewr eel pluh-ta vehrs
phrases.note: Il pleut à verse = it's pouring down. Verser means to pour, as when you pour a drink.

phrases.en: What do you want to do this weekend?
phrases.fr: Tu veux faire quoi ce week-end ?
phrases.ph: tew vuh fehr kwa suh wee-kend
phrases.note: The French really do say le week-end. Tu veux faire quoi ? is chatty; Qu'est-ce que tu veux faire ? is more standard.
On fait ... ? = Shall we do ...? It's a friendly way to suggest things. Un jeu = a game; the plural is jeux, with an x.
Se promener = to go for a walk, literally 'to walk yourself'. The se stays with on: on va se promener.

phrases.en: Shall we watch a film tonight?
phrases.fr: On regarde un film ce soir ?
phrases.note: Ce soir = tonight (this evening). Cette nuit means during the night, while you're asleep.

phrases.fr: Ce soir, on commande des pizzas.
phrases.ph: suh swar, ohn ko-mahnd day peed-za
phrases.note: Commander = to order food or goods. Des pizzas is plural because French doesn't say 'pizza' as a general, uncountable meal.

phrases.en: We're going to Grandma's on Sunday.
phrases.note: Chez = at or to someone's home, so chez Mamie = to Grandma's. No word for 'on' is needed before dimanche.

phrases.en: Do you want to come with us?
phrases.note: Tu veux + verb = Do you want to ...? Just add any verb in its dictionary form: tu veux manger ?
Être pressé = to be in a hurry. The n' is easy to miss when spoken because it blends into on.
Gagner = to win, and also to earn money. French uses the simple present qui gagne for 'who's winning'.
Literally 'it's to you'. The same words can also mean 'it's yours', so the context decides.
Sortir = to go out. Short and punchy: the present tense often covers things about to happen.
Tes = your, before plural nouns. Les chaussures are shoes, but les chaussettes are socks, so don't mix them up.

phrases.fr: Maintenant, on passe du temps en famille.
phrases.ph: mant-nahn, ohn pas dew tahn ahn fa-mee-y
phrases.note: Passer du temps = to spend time. En famille = as a family, all together.
Aller voir = to visit a person. Visiter is only for places like museums, never for people.

phrases.en: Turn that off and come outside.
phrases.note: Éteindre = to switch off, and also to put out a fire. The opposite, switching on, is allumer.

phrases.en: You're coming whether you like it or not.
phrases.fr: Tu viens, que ça te plaise ou non.
phrases.ph: tew vyan, kuh sa tuh plez oo nohn
phrases.note: Que ça te plaise ou non = whether you like it or not. Plaise is a special form of plaire (to please) used after que.

phrases.en: Some fresh air will do you good.
phrases.fr: Un peu d'air frais, ça te fera du bien.
phrases.ph: uhn puh dehr freh, sa tuh fuh-ra dew byan
phrases.note: Faire du bien = to do good. Fera is the future of faire, so ça te fera du bien = it will do you good.

phrases.en: You can't spend all day in bed.
phrases.fr: Tu ne peux pas passer toute la journée au lit.
phrases.ph: tew nuh puh pa pa-say toot la zhoor-nay oh lee
phrases.note: Au lit = in bed, with no word for 'the', just like English. Toute la journée = all day, literally 'the whole day'.
Midi = twelve noon; midnight is minuit. French tells the time with il est, literally 'it is'.

phrases.fr: Arrête de râler, ça va être marrant.
phrases.ph: a-ret duh ra-lay, sa va etr ma-rahn
phrases.note: Râler = to moan or grumble. Arrête de + verb = stop doing something: arrête de crier, arrête de râler.

phrases.fr: Allez, ne fais pas cette tête.
phrases.ph: a-lay, nuh feh pa set tet
phrases.note: Literally 'come on, don't make that face'. Allez here doesn't mean 'go' — it works like 'come on'.

phrases.fr: Tu t'ennuies ? Alors, range ta chambre.
phrases.ph: tew tahn-nwee a-lor, rahnzh ta shahnbr
phrases.note: Ranger = to tidy (put things away). Alors at the start works like 'then' or 'well' at the end in English.
On is everyday French for 'we'. Putting quoi (what) at the end is the relaxed way to ask at home.
On peut ... ? = Can we ...? Add any verb after it: On peut sortir ? On peut manger ?
Chez = at or to someone's house, so chez Mamie = to Grandma's. Mamie is the cosy word; grand-mère is more formal.
Du means 'some'. French needs it before food even when English says nothing: du pain, du pop-corn.

phrases.en: I don't want to watch that.
phrases.fr: Je ne veux pas regarder ça.
phrases.ph: zhuh nuh vuh pa ruh-gar-day sa
phrases.note: Ça = that, used constantly in speech. Je ne veux pas + verb = I don't want to do something.
Je peux ... ? is the easy way to ask permission — just raise your voice at the end. Choisir = to choose.

phrases.en: Can we go to the cinema?
phrases.note: Au = à + le, meaning 'to the' before a masculine word. You'll often hear au ciné for short.
Tricher = to cheat. French has no separate '-ing' form, so tu triches covers both 'you cheat' and 'you're cheating'.

phrases.en: What are we doing this weekend?
phrases.note: Qu'est-ce que = what, at the start of a question. French borrowed le week-end from English — keep the hyphen.
Literally 'I bore myself' — from s'ennuyer. Careful: je suis ennuyeuse means 'I'm boring'!

phrases.fr: Il n'y a rien à faire.
phrases.note: Il y a = there is; ne ... rien = nothing. So il n'y a rien à faire = there's nothing to do.

phrases.fr: Je peux faire la grasse matinée ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh fehr la gras ma-tee-nay
phrases.note: Faire la grasse matinée = to have a lie-in, literally 'to do the fat morning'. Teens shorten it to la grasse mat'.
False friend: rester means to stay, not to rest. Rester au lit = to stay in bed.
Literally 'am I obliged to come?', the everyday way to ask this. Obligée is for a girl — a boy says obligé.

phrases.fr: On peut faire quelque chose de sympa ?
phrases.ph: ohn puh fehr kel-kuh shohz duh san-pa
phrases.note: After quelque chose, put de before the describing word: quelque chose de sympa, quelque chose de nouveau.

phrases.en: I don't want to go for a walk.
phrases.fr: Je n'ai pas envie d'aller me promener.
phrases.ph: zhuh neh pa-zahn-vee da-lay muh prom-nay
phrases.note: Avoir envie de = to feel like. Se promener = to go for a walk, and se becomes me to match je.

phrases.fr: J'ai déjà quelque chose de prévu.
phrases.ph: zhay day-zha kel-kuh shohz duh pray-vew
phrases.note: Literally 'I already have something planned'. Prévu comes from prévoir, to plan ahead.
Copines = (girl) mates. For boys or a mixed group say copains. Mes is 'my' before a plural word.
Une balade = a walk, the relaxed word. In teen speak trop means 'so' or 'really', not just 'too'.

phrases.en: It's the weekend, leave me alone.
phrases.note: Laissez is the vous form, for both parents; to one person it's laisse-moi tranquille. Cheeky — expect a reaction!
Literally 'can we order something to eat?' Commander = to order. Food to take away is à emporter.

phrases.fr: Je peux rester à la maison ?
phrases.ph: zhuh puh res-tay a la may-zohn
phrases.note: À la maison = at home. You can also say chez moi, which means 'at my place'.
Anniversaire means birthday, not only anniversary. Bon anniversaire is just as common.

phrases.en: What do you want for your birthday?
phrases.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu veux pour ton anniversaire ?
phrases.note: Ton, not ta, because anniversaire is a masculine (le) word. Veux comes from vouloir, to want.
Un vœu = a wish. The œ is o and e joined together as one letter. Fais is the command form of faire (to make or do).
Souffler = to blow. Une bougie is a candle — French has no extra word for 'out' here.
The two dots on the ë in Noël tell you to say the o and the e separately, not as one sound.
Bonne is the feminine form of bon, because année is a feminine word. French people keep saying it all through January.
Une fête = a party (it can also mean a festival or name day). On organise = we're organising.

phrases.en: Who do you want to invite?
phrases.note: Putting qui (who) at the end is how families ask at home. The textbook version is Qui veux-tu inviter ?
Tu as signé covers both 'have you signed' and 'did you sign' — French uses avoir + signé for both.
Un cadeau becomes des cadeaux: words ending in -eau add x, not s, when there's more than one.

phrases.en: I can't believe you're fifteen already!
phrases.fr: Tu as déjà quinze ans, je n'arrive pas à y croire !
phrases.ph: tew a day-zha kan-zahn, zhuh na-reev pa-za ee krwar
phrases.note: French says 'you have fifteen years': age always uses avoir, never être. Y croire = to believe it.
The French birthday song is simply called Joyeux anniversaire. On chante ... = let's sing ... at home.
What French parents say to get a merci out of a child. Literally 'what does one say?' — on can mean 'one' or 'people'.
Dis is the command form of dire (to say). You need à before the person: dire merci à quelqu'un.
L' = it, squeezed in before the verb in a 'don't' command. Pas encore = not yet.

phrases.en: Don't invite too many people, OK?
phrases.fr: N'invite pas trop de monde, d'accord ?
phrases.ph: nan-veet pa troh duh mohnd, da-kor
phrases.note: Trop de monde = too many people — le monde means 'people' here, not 'the world'. D'accord = OK.

phrases.fr: La fête se termine à onze heures.
phrases.note: Se terminer = to finish, for events. French often uses the 24-hour clock, so you may hear vingt-trois heures too.

phrases.en: Who's going to clear all this up?
phrases.note: Qui va + verb = who's going to ... ? Tout ça = all this or all that, a very handy spoken phrase.

phrases.en: Go and get changed, the guests are coming.
phrases.fr: Va te changer, les invités arrivent.
phrases.note: Se changer = to get changed; te matches tu. Va (go) loses its s in commands: va, not vas.

phrases.en: Don't eat all the crisps before they get here.
phrases.fr: Ne mange pas toutes les chips avant qu'ils arrivent.
phrases.ph: nuh mahnzh pa toot lay sheeps a-vahn keel-za-reev
phrases.note: Les chips are crisps in France — chips are les frites. Toutes has -es because les chips is feminine plural.
Faire une fête = to have a party. French often uses faire where English says 'have' or 'make'.
Ouvrir = to open, and it follows je peux straight away with no word for 'to'.

phrases.en: I'd like new trainers for my birthday.
phrases.fr: J'aimerais de nouvelles baskets pour mon anniversaire.
phrases.ph: zhem-reh duh noo-vel bas-ket poor mohn-na-nee-vehr-sehr
phrases.note: Des baskets = trainers. J'aimerais (I would like) sounds more polite than je veux (I want).

phrases.en: When are we putting the tree up?
phrases.note: Le sapin = the fir tree, what French families call the Christmas tree. Faire le sapin = to put it up and decorate it.

phrases.fr: Il reste combien de jours avant Noël ?
phrases.ph: eel rest kohn-byan duh zhoor a-vahn no-el
phrases.note: Il reste = there are ... left. Combien de = how many, always followed by de before the noun.
Du gâteau = some cake. The little hat on â often marks an s that has dropped out over time.
Merci pour + a thing = thanks for. Before a verb it's usually merci de: merci de m'aider.
Offrir = to give as a present. Vous because the teen asks both parents; to one it's tu m'as offert.
L' = it (the present), placed before the verb. Adorer is stronger than aimer, which can sound lukewarm.

phrases.en: It's not what I asked for.
phrases.fr: Ce n'est pas ce que j'avais demandé.
phrases.ph: suh neh pa suh kuh zha-veh duh-mahn-day
phrases.note: Demander already means 'to ask for', so no extra word for 'for'. Watch the tone — this sounds ungrateful!
Inviter takes the person directly, with no à in between: inviter Lucía, inviter mes copines.
Ma fête d'anniversaire is literally 'my party of birthday'. Spoken French often tacks the topic on at the end like this.
La déco is short for la décoration. Faire la déco = to do the decorations.
Contente is for a girl — a boy says content. Avoid je suis excitée here: it can sound awkward in French.
Avoir hâte = to be really looking forward to something. The h in hâte is silent, but you don't run it together with j'ai.
Mon, not ma, because anniversaire is masculine. Feminine words starting with a vowel also take mon: mon amie.

phrases.fr: S'il vous plaît, ne chantez pas.
phrases.ph: seel voo pleh, nuh shahn-tay pa
phrases.note: Vous and chantez because it's said to both parents. To just one: s'il te plaît, ne chante pas.
Faire honte à quelqu'un = to embarrass someone, from la honte (shame). Vous because it's aimed at both parents.

phrases.fr: Mes copines peuvent dormir à la maison ?
phrases.ph: may ko-peen purv dor-meer a la may-zohn
phrases.note: Peuvent is the 'they' form of pouvoir (can). Dormir à la maison = to sleep at our place.

phrases.en: Can you stay upstairs during the party?
phrases.fr: Vous pouvez rester en haut pendant la fête ?
phrases.ph: voo poo-vay res-tay ahn oh pahn-dahn la fet
phrases.note: En haut = upstairs and en bas = downstairs. Pendant = during.
Fatiguée is for a girl — a boy is fatigué. The extra e changes the spelling but not the sound.

phrases.en: What time are you going to bed?
phrases.fr: Tu vas te coucher à quelle heure ?
phrases.ph: tew va tuh koo-shay a ke-lur
phrases.note: Se coucher = to go to bed, literally 'to lay yourself down'. À quelle heure ? = at what time?

phrases.en: You need to go to bed.
phrases.note: Tu dois = you must or you need to, from devoir. Te stays in te coucher because it's the tu form.
A fixed phrase worth learning whole: il se fait tard = it's getting late. The d in tard is silent.
Avoir cours = to have lessons, the natural way to say you've got school. The s in cours is silent.

phrases.en: Go and get ready for bed.
phrases.fr: Va te préparer pour aller te coucher.
phrases.ph: va tuh pray-pa-ray poor a-lay tuh koo-shay
phrases.note: Se préparer = to get ready. 'Go and do' is simply va + verb in French — no word for 'and'.
French says les dents (the teeth), not tes dents, because te already shows whose teeth they are.
Verbs with se, like se brosser, use être in the past: tu t'es brossé. No extra e even for a girl here, because les dents come after.
Lâcher = to let go of — a bit blunt, like 'drop it'. Le portable is the everyday word for a mobile.
Mets is the command from mettre (to put). The charger itself is le chargeur.
Éteindre = to switch off; the opposite is allumer. The s at the end of éteins is silent.

phrases.fr: Ne te couche pas trop tard.
phrases.ph: nuh tuh koosh pa troh tar
phrases.note: Literally 'don't go to bed too late'. In a 'don't' command, te stays in front of the verb.
Encore here means still, not again. Réveillée is for a girl — a boy is réveillé.

phrases.fr: Pourquoi tu ne dors toujours pas ?
phrases.ph: poor-kwa tew nuh dor too-zhoor pa
phrases.note: Toujours usually means always, but toujours pas means 'still not'. So: why are you still not sleeping?
Dors is the command form of dormir (to sleep). Adding maintenant (now) makes it firmer.
Bonne nuit is only for bedtime. Bonsoir means 'good evening' and is used when you arrive somewhere.
Dors bien to one person, dormez bien to several — the vous form of dormir.
